div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 4. 18 86.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 4. 18 86.
NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, U...0RT1-
CLTURF, c.

In all the principal grain-growing countries of Europe, according to the latest reports, the crops are less abun- dant than they were previously represented to be, and the quality is complained of, as a rule, even when the quantity is satisfactory. • It, is estimated that there are over 1,006 head of cattle held by half a dozen stockmen in the Westbourne dis- trict, which promises soon to become fin important point in this industry. The Manitoba and North-Western Railway are erecting cattle yards for the convenience of shippers. The famous shorthorn bull, "4th Duke of Clarence " (33597). calved October 28, 1874, is still to be seen at Bow Park, Brantford, Ontario, • almost as fresh and smooth as a young steer. He has been of great value to the herd, and must have been well taken care of to be in his old age, after hard service, in such fine, healthy con- dition. ' ' • There are 3,700,000 cows kept for milk purposes in the United Kingdom. Estimating at 440 gallons as the yield for the season per cow; the total is 1,628,000,0001ga110ns of milk. Of this 725,000,000 gallons are consumed in Ivarious ways, leaving 900,000,000 gallons to be converted into • cheese and butter. This is equivalent to 126,000 Itone of cheese and 89,285 tons of butter. The churning of whole milk finds little or no favour lamqng practical dairymen. The practice of creaming Ig_he'Ffilk and chnrning the cream only produces the most Vatisfactdry results. The system that makes it possible to skim the milk sweet is best; either deep, cold:setting or the centrifrugal separator. Sweet skim-milk for feeding' syock, or in 'domestic economy, fully pays for the extra labour expended. Close upon 400' pedigree Clydesdales have been ex- ported to Canada, the United States, and South Americ. during this season; and one of the largest shipments ever made left the Clyde recently by the Alcides. This steamer had on board fully 100 head of draught horses, of which more than 75 per cent. were Clydesdales. Ex- ' elusive of this shipment, Mr. Edward Pinnell has shipped three handsome horses from Liverpool to Buenos Ayres. One of the most important Clydesdale sales made this season has just been completed by Mr. William Mont- gomery, whose famous prize mare Ella, winner of the first prize at Edinburgh in July last,. has been purchased by Mr. Maclennan, from Buenos Ayres, on behalf of a South American buyer. Mr. Maclennan has also made several other purchases of horses and mares throughout the country, including the horse Star of Belton (4032), froth Mr. Ralston, Glamis. 4 THE FORTHCOMING BRITISH DAIRY SHOW.--«-The schedule of prizes at the eleventh annual show of the British Dairy Farmers', Association, on October sth, 6th,, 7th, and Bth, has been prepared, and it is Certainly the most compre- hensive that has yet been issued. There are eighteen classes for Cows and heifers, to be judged ,by appear- ance, the lateeds xecognised being Shorthorns; Jerseys, Guernseys, Red Polled, Keiries and Dexter Kerries, Welsh, and any other variety. As in former Tears. there are special classes for Jersey heifers bred in Great Brit ain or Ireland, and the English Jersey Cattle Society give a gold medal for the best cow or heifer in milk, bred in Great Britain or Ireland. The English Guernsey Cattle Society give three silver Medals for cows, heifers, ;and bulls bred, in England. ; In the milking trials 'there are four sections, with champion prizes. For bulls there are four classes—Shorthorns, Jerseys, Guernseys, and any Other pure breed. Pigs have ten classes, the, National Pig Breeders' Association presenting two champion prizes. Five classes are made for goats, and the British Goat Society give two extra prizes for J3tock 'registered by the society. The prizes for live stock are very hand- some, and numerous premiums of value are given for butter, che, and utensils.' •

'utter, cheese, __Jilt% DAIRY CATTLE.—In a paper read by Mr. 'lsaaa N. Ed- wards, of St. Albans, , Herefordshire on "Winter Dairy- ing," the writer says, as to the description of a dairy cow This is a vexed question, but I have come to the conclusion that the pedigree Shorthorn cow is as good as any for the dairy farmer. This may seem a startling assertion. Of course* we have all our fads.' Some prefer the Guernsey, some the Jersey, and,ll be- lieve, some the Dutch, but my reasons for preferring the pedigree Shorthorn are as follow,:—I can obtain as good an average of milk from them as from common Short- horns. For instance, my cow 'Fame' was in milk 341 days, and gave 9,170 lb. of milk: 'Matchless the sth' was in milk 280 days, and gave7,9os lb. of milk; Hya- cinth' was in milk ?80 days, and gave 9,190 lb. of milk; 'Lady White Flank' was in milk 423 days, and gave 10,825 lb. of milk. I have bought many common Short- horn cows, the best milkers I could obtain, and:paid quite as much for them, on the average, as ,for my pedi- grees, but only in one instance did a common Shorthorn exceed my best pedigree in her yield of milk. :Then, again, if there should be anything the matter with the cow, the pedigree is sure to be in good condition; while the common Shorthorn, fed on the same food, is always poor, and the. butcher will give £5 to ED more for the pedigree than for the common Shorthorn. Youl can make £lO at least of a pedigree calf at two months old, whilst you must keep the ordinary calf ten months be- fore you can make that amount. And, lastly, you are able to have an annual sale of your young stock, at which yoU can realise at feast double what can be ob- tained for ordinary Shorthorns of the same age although the lattercost you just the same to rear.. Therefore, for these reasons, I prefer The pedigree Shorthorn for the dairy farmer. As to the. bull, I am clearly of opinion that it is of name breeding from good cows unless. you have the right sort of bull.; I make it a rule never to use a bull unless I have personally examined its dam and sire, and, it possible, its grantfdam and sire. of the former throws additional interest upon the latter, which indicates that the te9dency is to develop stock rearing and curtail corn growing. The feeling that "there is safety in stock rearing" is gaining strength, and we fear that the returhs 0f71886 will still further shake con- fidence in the old, easy-going industry of corn raising. , Indeed, since the disastrous year of 1879 there has been no harvest quite so disappointing as that now in full swing. The wheat crop pulled up. considerably as the ripening season advanced, but only in exceptional cases will it reach an average yield. Our contemporary re- ceived 216 reports from -English counties, and in 70 per cent of these the ..wheat crop is said to be "under average," in 24 per cent. "average," and only 5 per cent. "over average.' There is no mistaking the significance of this testimony, which is the gloomiest since 1879. till crop of 1883 being a degree better. With the miserable price now, obtainable the Wheat crop.will give a poor ac- count of itself this year, and those who curtailed their area of it wilgnot regret having done so. It will be seen that the area under wheat in the United Kingdom this year is 2,286,064 acres, being 7.8 per cent less than last year and ,14.6 per cent, less than in 1884. Barley is better Upon the whole than wheat, but, we fear that the quality is not quite what could be desired. Of the returns relating to barley 48.5 per cent are "under aterage," 33.2 per cent. "average," and 23.9 per cent. "over average," which compares well"with 1879, but badly with all the inter- vening harvests. This year barley covers 2,241,266 acres —a few acres (0.7 per cent.) under last year, but 3.3 per cent. in, excess of the area in 1884. The oat crap in England is scarcely equal to that of barley, but decidedly superior to wheat-48.5 per cent. "under average," 38.9 per cent. "average," and only 12.6 per cent "over average." This is worse than in 1879, but not so bad as the oat harvest of 1881—just about equal to that of 1881. Oats are increasing in area. This year they occupy 13,081,701 acres, being 4.8 per cent. over last year, and 51 per cent. over 1881. Beans and peas- are uneven, but on the whole fairly satisfactory. As to root crops, we are happy to be able to say the reports all round are very favourable. Food for stock is abundant. We had hoped that a greater increase would be shown in the number of cattle' than the returns indicate. It now reaches 6.646,785 head, which is 6 per cent, more tlan in 1881, but only 01 per cent. over the number of last year. It would thus appear that the increase which get in is not being maintained. 'And in sheep, lambs, and pigs a steady decline is going on. The stock of sheep numbers 16,176,410 eing22 percent. less, than last year, and 1.3 per cent less than in 1884; lambs, 9,344,924, or 6.5 per cent. below last year, and 3.5 per cent. less than in 1884;. pigs, 2,221,557, which shows a'reduction from last year of 7.6 per cent., and of no less than 14 per cent. from 1881.

div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING,

It should be borne in mind that whatever kinds of I vegetables are exhibited; moderate sized samples that are young and tender should have precedence of the aged and tough, however large they may be. Even a moderate sized potato is preferable to an extra large ode, as the latter must be cut in order to boil it properly; and cut potatoes never look so niceon the dish as whole ones. In many instances Urge tubers have a cavity in the centre, and a judge having the curiosity to sever one in two would put the whole down as of little value. Pota- toes with deep eyes should not be staged for exhibition, as it is estimated that there is considerable waste in them-when they come to be peeled. Peas vary in their outward appearance, so much so that it may be advisable to examine a few in order that an accurate idea may be 'formed of the nature of:the contents of the pods. Seine of the Telegraph type, will have their pads fully de- veloped before the peas are half swelled, and to pick them'in that state would be to court defeat at the exhi- bition. In others the peas seem to .fill the Ind as it de- velopes, and when the latter. is full grown the contents, are really getting old, or at any rate past their best. Most peas have what is termed bloom" on the pods, and if these are grasped in the hand in the ordinary way when gathered. it is rubbed off and they have a spoiled appeara.nce When picked for exhibition they should be taken off with a pair of scissors, with as little' handling as possible, and laid in a single layer on a smooth surface, in a box or basket When they come to be set up in the exhibition tent, take up each one by the stalk and a.rrange iri a conical pile, with the points outward. Beans should be discarded if there is the least sign of the "eye" of the seed blackening, .Scarlet Runners and French Beans should, when bent, snap clean off and notleave a piece of fibre behind. Carrots and turnips should be of uniform size and free from scars and other blemishes,. and it is wise to cut two or three to ascertain if they are hollow or stringy, as either defect wotifd reduce the chances of success, and some other vegetable should be substituted. But if after ,two or three-of the largest and -coarsest looking are cut and prove sound and sweet a bunch of such would score a number of points. Onions can scarcely be too large, providing theyare free from cracks and the necks not too thick. Celery is ap- preciated in proportion to. the quantity of blanched growth fit for use as.well as its crispness. The remarks made on the Carrot are applicable to Beet and Pb.rrsnips. Assuming that all the above are in fair form, they-would, after addinn brace of Cauliflowers, form an excellent selection frith cottager, and if he had good Cabbages he might exclude the Parsnips. Some attach considerable importance to a brace of Cucumbers, but in addition to tberdiaubt whether they are his own growing it is- ques- Um:al)* if they do not prove the man's means-more them his ability. A cucumber house or frame, to do-well, needs attention two or three times daily, in the way of ventilating and closing pp. <Many cottagers'gardenenre some diiitance from their dwellings and are. not visited more than once a dayrby the, owner or members of his family; so if they had' the means to purchase glass ac- comniodation they would be otherwise handicapped. Irti additiorato the above- the following were last year ex- ' hibited by -a cottager at a local .show in a class of ump I limited number or most complete collection :—.Spinacl4 Horse •Rallsh, Lettuce;Jbrusalem and Globe Artichokes and Vegetable Marrow; The latter, by the way, if good;.- mayat any time take the-place of Beetroot or Parsnips. THB -FRONT GARDBI4k—AS herbaceous plants go out or flower it will be observedthat in many instances ther are disposed to forth °nets -which should be carefully- separated and inserted as cuttings. Those that can be secured with rudimentary roots may not require any more care than to be shaded from the sun for a week or ten days, buiethose haviiigno sign of roots should have thiprotection of a frame or hand glass and be shaded as well. Many herbaceous plants, though hardy enough, , are rather short-lived, and need young ones to be propa- gated occa4i many to pregerve the stock in preference to dividing old roots. The Pyrethrums should be seen to at once, alse the double. Rockets, Marsh Feverfew, Lychnia Chalindonica, Agrostuna Coronica, and sundry I Campanulas, with others that may be named. Tun WiNnow.—Hydrangea Hortensis, a somewhat erratic plant—here carrying pale rose-coloured flowers ! and there paki blue—should,. as soon as the flowering I period is pa*. be stoodbutsid'e and attended to as to , water. The old flowers and' the-wood they are borne on should be out to the last pair-of eyes in order to secure a compact bushy plant. IT the pieces cut off are made 1 into cuttings and inserted4napots they will in time strike • roots. It is a-puzzle tiavegetable physiolbgists how to ! account for the diversity of colour in plants (propagated [ by cuttings) from the same parent, as some will be I shades of. blue;.ethers pink, and grown under precisely I similar circumstances.

THE NANNAN,:OAK.—TiIe Nannan Oak was for ages an object of superstitious dfead to the peasantry of Merio- nethshire. On the 13thahly,1:613, it fell suddenly to the ground, completely worn-out with age. A drawing had been made of this extraordinary tree by Sir-Richard Colt Hoare only a idwhoursbefore it fell. As it stood then it appears in this representation, pierced and hollowed by time, and bklsted by-the stroke of lightning. In the • neighbourhood' where it stood it was known as the Haunted Oak—the Spirits Rhsted Tree—or in 'Welshi. "Ceubren yr Ellyee," the. Hobgoblins' Hollow Tree. It owed its fearitil nams,to a circumstance well known ia- the history of that country: Rowel Sell?, a Welsh chief-L-. tian, and LorePof Nannan; was privately slain during 2,1 hunting quarrel- by• hit. consin, Owen Glyndwr, or Glea- dower, and hidden for- a. %tag time within its hollow,- trunk. This celebrated oak measured Mt. 6in. in cit. cunaference, and stood' on the estate of Sir Robert Wit, _ Hams Vaughan,- Nannan Park,Merionethshire, who, afer - its fall, had acvariety of utensils manufactured from its 1 wood, which- iA of a beautiful dark colour, approaching to ebony; and there scarcely a house in Dolgelly that . does not contain an- engraving of this venerable tree, framed with the wood_ At Nannan there are se7eral relics; amongst others- a frame containing an engiaved portrait of Pitt, and under it the- following motto:— I" Y Gwr fel y dtterwn a wynebodd y dymestl." "'This man, like the oak, faced the tempest." ABOUT AWTS.—Mt. Darwin, in speaking of the wender- , ful difference in size between what is regarded as the brain of the ant and that of man, says, Ants " coalmuni- , cate information. to each other, and several unitalor the ! same wark or games of play. Thayrecog-nise onaanother after a long absence; they build great edifices, keep them clean, close the doors in the evening, and post sen- ! tries; they make roads and even tunnels undbr rivers,. they collect food for eummunity,and when anlobject tco large for entrance is brought to the nest they enlarE,..c the door, and afterwards build it up again ;,they go cat to battle in regular bands andtfreely sacrifice their lives- for the common weal; they emigrate in accordance- with a preconeerted plan. they capture slaves." Dr. Lindsay,. in speaking of the white_ ant, say :—" They exhibit foresight in the construction of long clay chim- neys for communication with air, land, or both during inundations. Their edifices or construative wozks in- clude,galleries and ccrridors, magazines,_nurseries,.royal chambers, offices, ordinary rooms and egg-rooms,, floors and ceilings, pillars and other appurtenances. The agri- cultural or havestsing ant not only stores up seed, but cultivates the plants which are to Toovide it, and care- fully gathers in its crop at the right season. In the wet season the seed in the granaries is apt to get wet and to sprout; and, accordingly, on the first fine day the ants 10-ring out all the damaged grain and set it in the sun to dry, returning to the store only such as is uninjured. These ants may truly be said to cultivate their estates. They have grass paddocks. From their fields they clear all the herbage save aristidee stricta, a grain-bearing grass, called by Dr. Linoicura ant rice, and they sow the seeds of the same grass,"

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. THE NEEDS OF THE LAYING HEN. In order to secure the best results from the keeping of domestic poultry it is necessary to understand what are the conditions under which the fowls must be kept, and the treatment that must be dealt out to them. Without this the business can only be conducted on the rule of thumb method, which is seldom satisfactory to either birds or owner. Of course we do not mean that it is needful for every poultry keeper to enter into these questions very deeply himself if he has any guide that can be trusted. It is in this way that the many papers which have devoted portions of their space to the dis- semination of poultry knowledge have done so much good. They have placed at the disposal of the ordinary poultry keeper the very best knowledge attainable on the subject. There is, however, much to be taught and to be learned on this subject, even by the most experienced, chiefly in the direction of examining the whys and the wherefores of the various changes which arise in the production of flesh and eggs. And in endeavouring to learn what are the effects of the different conditions under which fowls are kept every contribution to our knowledge on these important matters is welcome, and it is pleasing to see that so many who are well qualified to deal with the subject are giving attention thereto. Some months ago a series of lectures were given in con- nection with the London Institute of Agriculture by Mr. Alex. Conans, secretary of the English Poultry Club, on poultry keeping. One of the lectures was on the laying hen and to this lecture we are indebted for the follow- ing interesting account of the progress which goes on in the production of eggs. What the hen requires in order to keep her body in working order and to produce eggs is a supply of air to breathe, of food to make good the waste constantly going on in the body, and a supply of heat to make up for the waste of heat constantly abstracted from the body by the outer atmosphere. To the process of bre e athin which is necessary for the purpose of revivifying the 6blood with the supply of oxygen, and for the getting rid of surplus carbonic acid in the human body, it is necessary that a process go on which is in all respects similar to that of burning. In this process a certain :portion of the fatty substances which are in circulation in the body are consumed. The oxygen of the air, in fact, when taken into the lungs, is brought into contact with the starch, the sugar, the fat„ the albumen, and the other carbon-containing consti- tuents of our food and of the tissues of the body, and thus a certain consumption of these carbon-containing constituents takes place, and the waste passes off by the lungs in the form of carbonic acid gas. There is also a certain amount of water passing off from the lungs on the air we breathe out. This has also to be supplied by the ft eaten. Every increase of exertion which the body undergoes increases the amount of respiration, and consequently increases directly the consumption of car- bon-consuming constituents in the lungs. It also has the effect of increasing the waste of the tissues throughout the body. Coming now to the question of food, it is found by those who have studied the matter that in order' for the human frame to be sustained with the least .possible amount of waste in the way of food, the proportion of the various elements necessary to sustain life in an aver- age sized man is as follows :—Water, 100 parts; flesh formers, as albumen, five parts; heat givers, as starch, 22 parts; salt, one part. Taking the case of a hen to be analogous to be that of the man in certain respects, we have these additions to make :—The hen, in addition to the ordinary work of life, if she be a laying hen, has to supply the constituents for the formation of an egg every second day. The constituents of an egg are Water, 71i- parts; albumen, 14 parts; fat, Rec., 1 parts; phosphates, &c., 1.4. part. It is evident, therefore, that in order to supply the hen with the food necessary for her own bodily wants and for the manufacture ofeggs, a larger proportion of albumen is necessary. It is not easy to ar- rive at the precise figures, but we may take it that, for an average supply of eggs, the proportion of flesh-formers to albumen must be increased to about one-half, in- stead,, of somewhat less than one-fourth the amount necessary merely to keep the body going. It wilt thus be seen that the food must be regulated in accordance- with the demand upon the fowl. It is for this reason most obvious that the food which would answer under one set of circumstances will not under another, and for this reason there has had to be a great change-in the kind of food supplied to birds in a state of domestic- ation as compared with those which are at liberty. Do- mestication has, in fact, altered the whole conditions of life, and with these altered conditions have come. changed needs. We do not, therefore, hold with the idea that what the fowls in a wild state would eat, naturally- , eat what must be best for them when domesticated. We' have altered the demands upon the fowls, and must alter accordingly the supply of food. Then, there is the formation of the egg7Tli-e7MI-7 an egg consists of carbonate of lime, or hard chalk, and forme about one-tenth the weight of the egg. Limo in some-form is necessary to make the shell, and the want of it MUMS egg-eating by the hens themselves. I have generally found the best plan is to keep a good big heap of lime-and rubbish in one part of the run, so that the fowls can help themselves whenever they feel inclined so to do. The very best thing for the formation of shells is old mortar, but, failing that, oyster shells should be broken up and mixed with the heap of rubbish. In this way there can be given all the materials needed for shell formation.- Nitrogen is also needed to be supplied to the fowl, but this is obtained from the grass and other forms of vege- table life which are so freely eaten by fowls. It is for this reasonthat a grass run should be regarded as a sine qua non forthe rearing of young chickens. They can be reared without a grass run if plenty of green food is supplied, but nothing can really supply the place of tender young grass. Sulpher in some form must also be given to fe'evis, for analysis shows that this article very largel-Fenters into the composition of the feathers. Of course, sulphur more or less is found in all foods, but during the moulting season it is very advisable to give some flowereof sulphur in the soft foode This is one of those things-that always ought to be in the possession of the poultry,keeper, for it is a very valuable addition to the food at almost all periods of the year, but espe- cially in the spring and autumn. Poultry need spring medicine almost as much as children, and the giving of it will be found quite as beneficial in one case as the 'other. Returning again to the question of green food, it I be welltro•state what are the best kinds, though all are good. There is nothing to equal Dettuces, and thisl ;splendid vegetable, may be g;ven either young or whenl to seed. This I place first. After lettuce we should -put endive, which is nearly as good,. and then young! ~eabbage, after which any other may be-taken as the op-- • portunities of the- poultry-keeper will; permit. It mar not be generally known that the seed of. the sun-flower.' a splendid addition to the food of poultry. These are-1 ,highly stimulating, and should be kept for the wintee; when they will be relished by ,the fowls and will have most beneficial effect on the laying of the fowls. ',Therefore, these who, have large or small gardens can at once have them ornamented, or otherwise, with this .eesthetic fiowereand be providing an admirable food far- -their fowls. SEASONABLE HINTS. Some of the-young fowls will now be quite ready-to ',transfer to the hoes used for the larger fowls, and will know for the first time what it isto have a perch-eto rest upon. Asgreat mistake is often-made by havingthe ehes toe-narrow and too high. The result of the first _a crooked breasts,. which are so objectionable in a sitow !pen, often throwing out a bird otherwise first-rate, and • which are equally objectionable on the table, thus :Toil- •ing the appearance of the bird botlealive and dead.. For a perch a good- fir pole about three inches in diameter is the best; or failing that, a round pole of the -same diameter, but never less. Strips oferood, square, orreven Cornered, ought never to be used.,_ A high petch is-Detest objectionable; because heavy fowls injure themselves in 'getting dOwn.therefrom. For light fowls the height of the perch-in a large house is of no moment, but for heavy birds thiepercla should not be eaore than 18in. re:ove the •grounde

Greening, Gibson, Blackhurst, Jolley, Voisey, Forster, Isherwood, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Clarke, Hibbert, Eekersley, Broadbent, Heaton, Bonnel, Owen, Wright, C. Broadbent (ex-officio) • J. C. Sut- ton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk). THE MAINTENANCE OF THE WORKHOUSE MASTER'S CHILDREN. With regard to the subject of the maintenance of the children of the workhouse master (Mr. Mackey 1, which was considered by the Board at the previous meeting, the House Committee reported that they had had before them the letter which the clerk had been directed to send to Mr. Mackey. and also had an explanation from Mr. Mackey, tiee substance of which is given in the letter from Mr. Mackey to the chairman of the Board given below. The minutes of the committee concluded with the statement that they (the committee) csuld not gather from the master the exact reason for his payment of the 3s per week per child. The letter, which contains Mr. Mackey's explanation, was sub- seep:rangy read as follows In reply to the clerk's report as to the maintenance of our children, I beg to say our eldest (George Edward) has been living away from here since he was three years old, and has gone to the Grammar Sckool since he was seven, residing in the neighbourhood. Our next (Henry, 13 years of age) has gone to the same school for five years past, and has most, of his meals with his brother, so that they may be brought as much as pos- sible in contact with each other. The next two children (Charles and Herbert William, aged respectively 11 and 9) have their meals with us and go to the People's College, and for them I have paid regularly every half year since the order was made at the rate of 63 per week for every week whilst here. As the accounts are made up and closed the first Saturday after the 25th March and 29th September each year, I have paid to the treasurer the amounts due. The payments up to March last had been £4l 103; next payment the end of this month. In each summer half-peer the boys had been away on holidays for several weeks together, the date of their going and return- ing having been duly recorded at the time by the Hoisse Committee since July 1884. Of , course I had not paid for the weeks they were away. Since the order was made we have had another child born which is now nearly three years old, so that is all the family, ourselves included. What I now wish to point out to you is that the master and matron have rations allowed them according to the specified scale similar to the other officers and inmates. I have made it a rigid rule both be- fore the order was made and since not to draw anythin from the stores beyond that scale, and whenever we re- qnired anything more for ourselves and children I got it from my private means If anyone doubts this the clerk has rov books sent to him regularly, and if I have at any time overdrawn this specified allowance he is in a position. easily to point it out to you. There are many things _I would wish to say but don't like to trouble you, with too long a letter, so will conclude by saying that if it would be more satisfactory to you I would much prefer a money allowance in lieu of the rations. Wtiatever Ido is always frank and honourable, and such expressions on the part of the clerk are Quite nucalled for."—Mr. VOISEY, in moving the adoption of the House Committee's minutes, said the impression he had formed at the previous meeting of the Board when the matter of the maintenance of the Workhouse Master's children• was before them, was that Mr. Mackey was supplying his children from the stores of the Workhouse, and that order of March,•lBB3, that he ~laould pay 33 per week per child was made to recoup the Guardians for the outlay in respect of the children. It had, therefore, been a matter of surprise to him when Mr. Mac- key explained at the committee.meeting that he had never supplied his children out of the Workhouse stores. When asked why he had made the payment of 33 per week in respect of two of the children Mr. Mackey said he could not tell. He ( Mr. Voisey) asked him if it was for the privilege of having them sleeping under the roof of the Workhouse, or for having their linen washed, but he could not tell them clearly. If Mr. Mackey's ex- planation was right he had been supporting the children himself all the time, and two of them had only been there occasionally on a visit to himself. If that were so 3s a week was a rather extreme sum to set down for each child. He Wished the clerk would explain how the arrange- ment for 3s was come to.—The CLERK said it was because no other arrangement would be legal, and pointed out that the orders were that when the children of'a workhouse master lived in the- workhouse something had to be paid for their maintenance.—Mr. VOISET said that the master said in his letter that two of the children had been in the workhouse only occasionally. He thought it would be un- fair to impose 3s per week for each child if he only saw them now and tnen, and they only occasiona)ly slept at the workhouse.—The Cenenx,said the Beard had resolved sim- ply this—that there should be an account presented of the children residing at the workhouse since the date of their resolution, and that that account should be clear to the Guardians and to the auditor. This matter had come up on the auditor's complaint. He had complained to the Local Government Board; be had complained to loim (the clerk) both by letter and personally over and over again because the matter was not made clear. He might tell them that statements had been made that there were, three children resident in the workhouse.. It was for the auditor to deal with

• that matter, and he might ask the Local Government Board to send Me. Henley down to have the whole of the officers before him: The Calvelsn explained that the rations al- ilbwed the master and matron and other officers were fixed on a maximum scale, but it was clearly laid down that any that might be left afterthe officer bad been satisfied be- longed to the Union.andbot to the officer.-e-Mr. GREENING seconded the adoption of- the minutes, and said he had been surprised when Mk Mackie told them that he did , not draw any of the maintenance of the children, for whom he paid. Mr. Mackey told , them that he 'paid for two children; and that the oaher two were Iliving away. It had been suggested that morning by rao,me one that there were three children living there besides :the infant, but Mir Mackey distinctlystold them there were '-eniy two, and that when they were short of provision over his ration they bought be remainder. Ire should like to , know for a fact whether there were two or three children.— The CHAARMAN, referring to Mr. Mackey's•letter. said there were three children besidee• the infant.—Mr. Cuantrn said . that he understood when. Mr. Mackey made his explanation that the second boy was, living with', the eldest boy.—Mr. GIRINNING : We all unarstand it that way; we were led to believe that the two children were sleeping away.—The CLERK said he was told -that a pauper took the second child to school everyanornicg.Mr. OwnNssaid that the master and matron would not be justified to draw the maximum amount of their rations'-in order that others might eat with thern.—Mr. GIBSON mld. at one time, when Mrs. Mackey ha an increase of salary or £l5, one of the. reasons given for it was that she bad to pay for her childrem. It seemed to him (Mr. Gibson) that either Mr. Mackey was a fool or he thought the Gaardians fools., (Laughter.)—The minutes of ;the House COmmittee- wens then passed. The porterWbook bearing been sent for,. Mr. GIBSON said that the names of the Master's children bad not been en- tered in the book when they left ozaentered the workhouse. —The Porter (Mr. Clirry) was then calked into the ram, land in reply to the Chairman aaid he bad never received linstructions to enter the names •of .the Master's children.— The CHAIRMAN: Ilaur instruct-lone are to book everybody. How many children are there here ?—The PORTER: There are three sleeping here but one ot them sometimes sleeps outside.—Mr. G Bagli -Does the eldest ever come here.— The PORTBR : Oh, yea, be comes every evening; hssome- times sleeps here.—The Crazazsaid the only infcra-nation be could get was from the porter's book, but the informa- tion oa this matter was not there.. Was it not a tact that the boys bad gene inte the Workhouse, stopped all, night, and gone away in the rcerningc—The PORTEL Ytt3.— At teiNsome farther remarks,,thePorter was instructed, to en- ter the names of,the child:en in his book, when‘ tht7 en. tered or left the Workhouse in future—The Porter having retired, the CLpaax said he did not wish it to a?pear that the Porter was to blame far not entering the names of the children without having had distinct instructions So that eflact, He did not know but what the Porter bad taken a correct view oi his dutie.a.--Mr. GREENING thought the Porter had answered the questions very satisfactorily.—At a later rtage of the meeting Mr..Voism moved the fc-llowing reso- lution with regard to the subject, viz :—" That the official auditor of te Workhcase or Guardians' accounts be asked to institute an inquiry.:.l. Whether Mr. Mazkey, the rms.. lter, has come under any liability to the Guardians for tha. t,maintenance and res!dence-ot- any of his children under the "order of the Board of Guardians of March, 1/3.83. 2. If ers for what amount, and what &was be has paid on account of that liability." This motion was seaonded by Mir. Bacian-miT, and agreed,to. The discnssk.,-a, on the subjact then closed.

ARLETTE. A MAN'S REMEMBRANCE. The day is spent, and fields new-shorn, Are bright with fading sheen; Like blossoms left behind the corn, The maidens come and glean; Blue eyes, and floating locks of gold, Have caught you in their net; Ycu smile, and call me strange and cold— You never knew Arlette. Ilmet her when this life of mine Had turned from sweet to sour; There was no sparkle in the wine, No bloom upon the flower. I:roamed away to bear alone The stings of vain regret; The grain was gone, the reapers flown, When first I found Arlette. The glamour of the "sunny south" .About her beauty lies; A mellow cheek, a scarlet mouth, And dark, beseeching eyes; 1, A daughter of the soil, as sweet As summer buds dew-wet; No taint of our town-bred deceit Has ever touched Arlette. With half her charm some girls might win A fashionable fame; How came she with that southern skin, And soft old Norman name? . We talked I questioned, she replied, • Till I forgot my fret; For bitter thoughts and angry pride • All fled before Arlette. How ends the tale? To your surprise There is no end to tell! I left no tears in those dark eyes, f=r, Although I loved them well; ... Her picture hangs within my brain 4 • Fresh and unsullied yet; No empty vows of mine shall pain The heart of true Arlette. • But when my harvest-field appears As bare as it can be, She comes, and finds some golden ears Of life's good grain for me; My old belief in truth and trust She brings back, sometimes yet; You smile again ;—ah,.well, you must; ' You never knew Arlette. —Good Words.
SiRAH DOIJDNBY.

- - - - - - A man must becothe wise at his own expense. Be brief; for it is with words as with sunbeams, the more they are condensed the deeper they burn. Cunning is not the best nor the worst of our qualities;. It floats between virtue and vice. Speaking of Switzerland,. its scenery is remarkably fine, but its climb-it is very rough. Statistics are said t,o shOw that in the whole of Europe the women have a majority of 4,579,000. A contemporary has for a headline, ".Why are wives -- -what they are?" We can't tell unless it is because they are married. Since not only judgments have their errands, but mercies their commissions, snatch not at every favour, nor think thyself passed by, if they fall upon thy neigh- bour.—Sir Thos. Bro-wne. I count these things to be grandly true : , That a noble deed is a step toward God. Lifting the sonl from the common sod To a purer air and a broader view. The Eternal God deals with us one by one, each one in his own way; and bystanders may pity and com- passionate the long throes of our travail, but they can- not aid us except by their prayers. Keep to the right, as the law directs; Keep from the world thy friend's defects; Keep all thy thoughts on purest themes; Keep from thine eyes the motes and beams; Keep true thy deed, thy honour bright; Keep firm thy faith in God and right; Keep well from any sin and stain; Keep from the ways that bring thee pain. Often the cockloft is empty in those whom nature hath built many storeys high.—Thamas Neither borrow money of a neighbour, or of a friend, but of a stranger; where, paying for it, thou shalt here no more of it.--"-Burleigh. • Everything in nature grows either healthy or un- healthy; and character is no exception. It is either ex- panding intomew and more lovely forms or it is tough- ening into deformity. It is either ripening into richness and sweetness or shrivelling into crabbed bitterness. The briefest marriage ceremonies in the _world—that is among civilised nations—are those practised in the United States of America. The following is authentic: —Magistrate: "What is your name, sir ?'—Answer: "Matty."—Magistrate : "What is your name, miss ?" Answer: "Polly."—Magistrate: "Matty-. do you take

Polly ?"—Answer : " No-mistake."—Magistcate: "Polly, do you take Matty ?"—Answer: "I reckon I do."— Magistrate: "Well, then. I pronounce you man and wife all the days of your life." "W—, do you know why you are like a donkey?"— "Like a donkey !" echoed W—, opening his eyes wide. "No, I don't."—" Do you give it up ?"—" I do."—" Be- cause your better half is stubbornness herself."—" That's not bad. Ha! ha! I'll give that to my wife when I get home." "Mrs. W—,' he asked, as he sat down to supper, "Do you know why lam like a donkey ?" He waited a moment, expecting his wife to give it up. But she didn't. She looked at him somewhat commisserat- ingly as she answered, "I suppose because yoti; were born so." An old Dutch farmer, just arrived at the dignity of justice of the peace, had his first marriage case. He dished it up in this way. He first said to the man,;" Veil, you vents .to be marrit, do you? Veil, you loves dis voman so goot as any voman you have ever; see?" "Yes," answered the man. Then to the woman, "Veil, do you love dis man so better ad no man you never see?" "Lady hesitated, .and he repeated. " ;do you likes him so yell as to be his rife ?" "Oh, certainly." she answered, with a kind of a titter. "Veil, dat is all any reasonable man can expect. So you are marrit ; I pronounce you man and vile." The man then asked the Justice what was to pay. ." Oh, nothing at all, nothing at all; you. are welcome to it if it Will do you any goot." The young elephant watched him with great interest, apparently amused at the bright bits of colour. The painter was absorbed in his work when the dinner- bell rang. He put his pot and brush down, and went off to his meal. The elephant waited till he was out of sight, then carefully felt for the brush with his trunk. A QUESTION,OF RELIEF.

Mr. EhttontrßsT said an Act had been neeently pasaed to reliexe Guardians from making any asrangements be- tween men and their wives who had disagzeed. If a wan and his wife could not ar ee they came to the Board, and arrangements were made through the officers for the man to pay for the maintenance of the woman, and then the officer had to get the money back. That was a pernicious system, because in some cases the officer had to pay the woman every week and wait a long time before he got the money back. The magistrates had now to take the matter in hand, and the Board wete consequently relieved. He wished to know whether instructions had been given to the Relief Committee that they were no longer expected to deal with the cases. What would they do with the cases already in the hands of the officers ?—The CHAIRMAN I It is on the ground that the people are entirely destitute that we have tiken proneedings.—The CLERIC said Mr. Blackhurst had fairly put the question before the Board. Hitherto the wife came to the Board because she could go nowhere else, and the Board relieved her because she was destitute, and they

had taken their remedy agair,t tLie husband. nn Act been passed whico enabled tbe wife to go before the magis" trates and apply for an order without having to pass through the form of pauperism. -I return should be presented by the officers with resw!ct to the number of cases, and CO merit made by them on the desirability of their refusing re bet and referring the wife to the court.—The subject then dropped.

div.p: FOREIGN NEWS. THE BULGARIAN CRISIS. PRINCE ALEXANDER RELURNS TO BULGARIA.— EN IHUSIASTIC RECEPTION. LEmBERO, SAYDRDAY. Prince Alexander left here shortly after two e'clock this afternoon by special train for gournania. His resolve to return to Balgaria was. it is assumed, prompted by the despatches, which reached him in the morning by the hand of his brother, Prince Lonis. BuceranEsT, SUND.kY.--Prince Alexander arrived at ten o'clock this morning at the Northern Railway Station, where an immense crowd had assembled te welcome him. M. Bradano and the other Bulgarian Ministers; M. Ma- eherics, the Bulgarian Agent ; the principal Bulgarian residents, and Sir William White were on the plaiforrn to receive his Highness. The people repeatedly cheered the Prince. His Highness conversed for a short time with wove- rat persons, and at eleven o'clock proceeded by special train for Giurgevo, amid the cheers of the people. SISYCrYS., MONDAy.—Prince Alexander arrived here on board his yacht at eieht o'clock tnis morning, having left Rustchuk•at four o'clock. The reception accorded to his Highness at this place was more enthusiastic than at Rustchuk. The Prince's progress through the 'town was a continuous triumph, the people nnharnessing the horses, and carrying him on their ehoulders to the Greek Church, where a "Te Deum" was sung. The Pcince will leave at ten o'clock for Tirnova, where he will errive this -evening. VIENNA, SIINDAY.—Pastor Koch, the Prince't chaplain, sends the [(diming telegram to Vienna :—'• erince did not sign abdication. He only wrote the following words, 'Bog da soas.i Bulgaria' (God save Bulgaria.) " While in Lem- berg the Prince received over 000 telegrams from London, Vienna, Bulgaria, and Frazensbad. We have now authentic information that the real author of the conspiracy was Colonel-Zacheroff, the Russian military attache at Sofia, who in the name of the Czar promised the officers in the Bulgarian War Department that the Czer would have them transferred to the Retssian army with the same rank if they aided in the expulsion of Prince Alex- ander and allowed Russian Staff officers to come to Bals • garia.—Tintes. VIENNA, MONDAY.—The "Neue Freie 'Presse " to-day states that king Milan yesterday despatched a telegram to 'Prince Alexander. at Rustchuk, expressing warm sympathy with his Highness, as well as joy and •eatisfaction at his re- turn to Bulgaria. The same journal states that en the Prince's arrival at Bucharest, Genei Grecedo, the Prefect of the Royal Palace, was present to greet the Prince on behalf of the King of 'Roumania. VIENNA, MONDAY.—Apart from further details as to the • enthusiastic nature of the reception accorded to 'Prince Alexander on his arrival at Ruetchuklesterday nothing of importance has reached here from Bulgaria. to-day. That the Prince is not proceeding direct to Soda from the Danube as originally -proposed, but is proceeding thither vitt Tirnova and Phillipoppolis may be ascribed to the fact that the chief military force i 3 at Phillippopolis. Most probably the Prince will enter Sofia at the head of the troops, so as to guard against any possible surprise. M. Stambultiff- yes- terday placed the powers conferred upon him by the Re- gency into the hands of Prince Alexander. Prince Alex- ander of Reese, the father of the Bulgarian Ruler, In a • conversation with a high military personage, is reported to have expressed himself as follows :,`" Prudence forbade my son returning td Bulgaria, but honour and his duty as a Prince and soldier constrains him not to evade any danger that may be awaiting him in Bulgaria, even at the risk of his life. Now that he is returning, I look upon my son as lost, although I personally advised him to go where his duty called him.—" Standard." HOW THE‘:KIDNAPPED PRINCE WAS TREATED. In reply to a telegram addressed to him by the editor of the "Neue Freie Presse," asking for details, Dr. Koch, the Prince's chaplain, wired as follows :—" You want details. :Imagine what could be expected from drunken officers and soldiers, from the shameful rudenets of intoxicated Bul- gatians. Imagine all that amidst the din of artillery and musketry fire. and your readers will want no further details. The escort that accompanied the Prince to the Danube had orders to shoot him should he attempt to escape or address a word to anybody on the road. In the villages they tra- versed the inhabitants were threatened with death if they should appear outside their houses., or even at their win- dows. The crew on board the yacht insulted him, and obliged him to •beep inside his cabin. He remained 24 hours without food. At the stations along the Russian railway between Odessa and tbe Austrian frontier he was mocked and jeered at, and it was Only on reaching Aus- trian territory that he got news of the counter-revolntion. The officers of the Surican Regiment, of which his father is chief, Publicly insulted him on his tourney." 'PRINCE ALEXANDER'S 'PROGRESS. ELX/RA, WEDN'eSDay, 2 P M -- Prince Alexander and suite left Tirnova at two o'clock yesterday afternoon, and arrived here at eight in the evening. ';:Throughout his jour- ney his Highness met with the sameenthusiastie reception as previously. At every-village ha was met by the priest. and in every town 'by the clergy and principal citizens, who all assured the Prince of their elevotien to his person and cause. PHILLIPOPPOLIS, WEDNESDAY. Prince Alexander ar- rived here this morning, and, met with an enthusiastic re- ception from the crewds which thronged the streets. His Highness will protsattly reach Sofia on ;Friday evening. - RUSSIAN' THREATS AND lICTRIGUES. Sr. 'PETERSBURG. The "Novoe'Vremya" says that the iournev of Prince Dolgor- ouki to Bulgaria has been relincoriehed, owing to informa- tion received, accordiag to which the revelation of the 21st Inst. was without a thead, and was initiated without suffi- cient guarantees that it commanded the approval of the whole Bulgarian nation. PRANCE ALEXANDER AND TliE CZAR. The Ruesian "Official Messenger " has.printsd copies of two highly interesting telegrams, one being a despatch which Privce Alexander of Bulgaria addressed to the Czar from Rustchuk, and the other his Retsian 'Majesty's reply. The Prinei's telegram its couched in the most submissive: terms. lie, c3ncludeis by saying that Xussia having given him his crown, it is into the hands: of Russia's Sovereign rthat be is 'ready to reeler it. The Czar in his reply-says he cannot approve the Prine's return to Bulgaria, "foreseeing its sinister consequences for the country, which has been so severely tried: ' He promises to abstain from intervention "as long at the -Fence remains in Bulgaria," but "reserves to himself to Judge what his father's venerated memoryathe interests of Ruceia, and the , peace of Europe require of him." Latlia and Rand's magazins, situated on the outskirts of this city, containing 30 tons of dynamite, powder, and other similar substances, was ex- ploded by lightning last night. The shock was felt over the whole city, atd windows were broken in all parts. Eight othez magazines in the vicinity were destroyed, although their contents were not exploded. One man was killed, and a large number injured, the wounds of four being, it is be- lieved. mortaL NEW SOUTH WALES.—THE CENTENARY. Synwnv, MONDAY.—The Premier laid before Parliament on the 27th inst proposals for the celebration of the cen- tenary of New South Wales, in January, 1888. The Government purpose procle.iming a carnival season from January 'Z3, 1888, the anniversary of the first landing in the colony of Governor Phillip, until February ilth the latter being the anniversary of the proclamation of the Government. The carnival is to include special and appro- priate religious services, a ceremonial reception of visitors, a commemorative oration, an art exhibition, a musical fes- tival,nn agricultural, pastoral, industrial, and mining ex- hibition open to the British dominion; a military and naval review of all the colony's forces, an aquatic festival, an in- ternational regatta, a rifle match, a special race meeting, athletic sports. and excursions throughout the colony. The event will also be signalised by the opening of a me- morial hall and art gallery, a building intended for technical education, a free public library, and centennial and trades halls.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. The Earl of Rosebery and several other peers took the .oath and subscribed to the roll of Parliament. Ate INDIAN SUCCESSION CASE —Lord STANZEY Of ALDERLEY asked the Government if they would inquire into the circumstances of the reversing of the decision of the Bombay Government in favour of Sirdar Prithi Rao in his Zemindary.—The Marquis of SALISBURY stated that the case in question was one of succession dependingeupon the intricacies of the Hindoo law of adoption. If matters of this kind were to be discussed at all it should be .on general grounds, and not in respect of an individual case. Their lordships adjourned at 4-45. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. SUGAR BOUNTIES.—Lord R. Caterwaul.le in answer to a qoestion from Mr. Norris as to the investigitions of the Royal Commission on Trade and as to the cueletion of the sugar bounties, said the hon. gentleman had only to read the three reports of the Commission, and he would find that they had not made any suggestions in the direction he would wish. The Government were quite aware that the manufacturing interests ha connection with the sugar ques- tion had suffered from the operation of foreignobounties, but they were not in a position to state whether itoreas in their power to mitigate that injury. The honomember would emderstand that the Government had also to take into con- sideration the interests of the consumers—(ironical Opposi- tion cheers)—and he had never yet heard iie alleged that the consumers were injuriously affected by the operation of these foreign bounties. But it was under the-consideration -of the Government whether they could not advantageously recommence negotiations with foreign countries as to the -general operation of those bounties. MARRIAGES OF DISSENTBRS.—In answer to Mr:Shirley, the ATTORNEY-GENERAL said her Majesty's Government hoped to he able to introduce early next session a bill deal- 'lug with the question of the attendance of the registrar at .marriages in Nonconformist chapels. Tau 'QIIIISTION OF TITHES.—Mr. H. R. BARQUHARSON asked the Home Secretary whether the Government would consider the advisability of bringing in a bill next session' to make the payment of tithes by landlords compulsory.—. Mr. lalloomews replied that whether any alteration should be made in the existing law was a matter for the considera- tion of the Cabinet. e PERPETUAL PENSlONS.—Replving to Mr. Bradlaugh and ' Mr. Pickersgill, the CHANCELLOR of the ExCitEQUEU stated. that he proposed to ask the House to give precedence to . dovernment business next day. Even should Mr. Brad-' laugh obtain tbe appointment of a committee on the subject I of perpetual pensions, a committee could not proceed to ' werk this session, and the Government could not make an exception in favour of the motion. The Government were .quite sensible of the importance of the subject, and wouldi be perfectly prepared next session to grant the committee, he asked for. Until the hon. member's motion was dis-? posed of, no further pensions would be commuted. Now, however, we wereencouetered by a national uprising of the people, and in the coming cold weather we should have $0;800 troops employed in Upper Burmah, so that the war, instead of costing a few hundred thousands, would dust several .rail- liens. •Since the Indian Budget statement was made, the ex- ehangovalue of the rupee had fallen te is 41-d, which was equal to a loss to the Indian Treasury of one and a half millions nterling ; and if to-that they added two or three millions.this year for the Burmese war, they would involve India in a deficit of four milieus. He submitted that th e whole of this enormous burden should not he borne by a' countreesa poor as India. We .oecupied a position intUoper Burmah as hateful as that ofaFrance in Tonquin and in Madegasear ; and on behalf of the Liberal party he wished to express his horror and detestation at what was takicg place there. He warned,' the House that a cycle of farnicesenuet in the ordinary course be expected to occur in India, and unless greater attention was paid totindian finance in aefew years our greatdependency would .be in a condition little short of bankruptcy. Native discontent was directed.very largely against the costliness of our Qov- ernmett and , the habit of throwicg upon India expenses which did not.croperly belong to it, such as those &tieing from theeaby.ezinian, Egyptianaand Burmah wars. We. must change our policy in that respect if we were to avoid serious troulelesain the future. (Fiere hear.) Mr. FXCHANLIZ seconded the amendment. Mr. Gauelanmeoved as an amendment to Mr. Snaitlele ; amendment to oue:t all the wordo after "Burmah," in order'' to add—" and at learning that the Government have re- solved to persevere in their policy of „annexation, especially; as the native pepedation have by their active hostility and armed reaietance to the invading •forces shown that the,y t have no desire to line- under Britiehrule.' He submitted that no valid reasone had been given to justify the war..' Even were Wog Theebaw the dangerous person he was posed to be we could easily have soppier-led him by some member of the Buricese Royal Family. aa e should shortly have in Burnish a lareeer force than the• French had had in Tonquin, anti the efforts that we were .compelled to put forth showedohat we were invading the country against the , wishes of thedahabitatts. He regarded the war as an tin- 'righteous one. . ' Sir J. Goate intimated that a Blue Book,vc reld be shortly . published which woufel give full infoemation with regard to efearrnese affairee ..end, ie. discussing the amendments, he traced the histos of the war, and pointed out :that the late . Government, as well as their predecessors and the present Grorornment, hatlzorne to the conclusion that it was neces- sary for the safete- of 'British Burmali and the interest of .India. He denied that it was undertaken inaneag.gressive .epirit. He looked II:open:illy at the future of the country, and ftli, no reason why, in the course of a year or two, it should not ec quiet. Mr. Blane, Mr. Illingworth, Dr. Termer, Mr. Allisen, and Mr A. O'Connoropposed the acne-a-talon of Burmah, and objected te the cost of the war Leingettrown upon the Indian revenues. Sir U. Ic. A. The CrrAwcstt.on of the EXCHEQUER explained the course the Government intended to pursue, namely, to vote successively against both amendments. OR a division Mr. Cremer's amendment was negatived by 201 to 125, and Mr. S. Smith's amendment was negatived by WO to 126. Dr. CLARK then moved the adjournment of the debate, but the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER strongly opposed it, and remarked that the evening's discussion had not been conceived in the public interest.—Mr. T. P. O'Cornion rose to order and objected to this allegation, hut the :SPEAM3R 'declined to interfere ; and after a somewhat heated wrangle, in which the Chancellor of the Exchequer's des- cription of the debate was warmly repelled by Mr. hung- worth, Mr. A. O'Connor, and others, one,. Mr. J. Most- LE s advise the Government to give way—the motion was negatived on a division by 197 to 122 —Mr. PicroN then moved the adjournment of the House; and the CHANCEL. lOR of the EXCHE.UER said that having entered a necessary protest an behalf of the prosecution of business and ac- knowleZging the rights and power of a minority, the Government would offer no further objection to the de- bate being adjourned. The debate was accordingly ad- journed* Mr. Jackson introduced a bill abolishing the Secret Ser- vice Vrind. The House adjourned at 1,0. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his vat at 4-15.

There were only ten peers present. Lord DBNIMN introduced the Women's Suffrage Bill and it was read a first time.—On the motion of the Duke of Dm/um/aux and CzAsnos, the Standing 'Orders Com- mittee add the Committee of belection were appointed. The Earl of Dude took the oath and subscribed the roll. The House adjourned at 4-30. HOUSi3 OF COMMONS.—TunnIY. _ .

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE CHURCH or ENGLAND REVENUES. Mr. PICTON gave notice that next session he would move for the ap- pointment of a Select Committee to inquire into and report on the revenues of the Church of England as respects their nature, origin, amount, distribution, and applica- tion. TELEGRAPHIC MONEY ORDERS.--In -reply to Mr. Shir- ley, Mr. RAIRES said that he had notTet bad time fully to consider the proposed establishment of 'telegraphic money orders in the coantry, but he would give it his best atten- tion during the recess. There was a question as to provid- ing money to meet the demands at small offices; and there were various other difficulties which required very careful consideration. IRISH ,QIIESTIONS.—In answer to Mr. J. O'Connor, Mr. ASHMEAD BARTLETT said that works at Haulbowilne, for which .E 1,500 bad been provided in the egimates, had been ordered to be proceeded with.—ln reply to Mr. T. D. Sulli- von, Sir M; HICKS-BEACH said that be was informed that in the recent Belfast riots one constable had been killed and five officers and 36 men severely injured; 232 men of the force had been more or less injured, principally by stones, but in many cases these injuries were not at all serious. TRADE WITH BURMAII AND CHI:EA.—In reply to Mr. King, Sir Jsains FERGUSON said that the convention lately signed at Pekin had not yet been ratified, because it had not reached this cenntry in its formal shape. By that con- vention we had obtained the fullest recegnition by the Chinese Government of British rule in Upper Burmali ; we bad retained freedom of acCon with reference to our boun- daries; we had secured the frontier trade between China and Burmah, and opened up SouthMest China to our com- merce. THE BILFAST IsiQuinY.—ln reply to Mr. Sexton, the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER declined to interrupt the debate on the Address to proceed ,with the Belfast inquiry. There was nothing in the latter which should induce the hen. member to offer such opposition as would bring the bill within the operation of the half-past twelve rule. ("Hear.)

hibited to the house in a box an interesting collection of iron end other missiles said to have been used in the riots —On the motion of Mr. P. MACDONALD the debate Was ad- journed. BALE UNDER. LEGAL PROCESS.—Mr. E. RODEFiTSON .ob- rained leave to introduce a Bill to protect (to the value of £2O) from seizure or sale, under legal process, the necessary furniture. books. tools, wearing apparel, and bedding of a householder and his family. The Bill was read a first time. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack at a quarter to four O'clock. NEW PEERS —Viscount Cross of Broughton-in-Furness (Sir R. Cross). introduced by Viscount Hardinge and Lord Sidrnouth, and Lord Stanley of Preston (Sir F. Stanley), introduced by Lord's Harris and Bateman, took the oath and subscribed the roll upon their elevation to the peerage. Tun WOMAN'S SUFFRAGE BILL.—Lord DENMAN moved the second reading of the Woman's Suffrage Bill, which, be ssid, he should not so persistently press forward if it were not that he had the misfortune to be growing old. He had been for five years raising the question. He believed there were many members of both Houses ; who sympathised with the object he had in view, and lately he had, in deference to the opinion of some of its supporters, confined the bill to householders.—The LORD CHANCELLOR thought it would he impossible to say that the bill was a desirable one to introduce for discussion on the second of September, but he did not wish it to be supposed that in Moo vote he intended to give in opposition to the motion he committed himself against the principle of the measure.—The motion was negatived, and the bill thrown out without a divisiou. THE BErxisT RIOTS.—EarI DE LA WARE moved for a return of persons killed or wounded in the recent riotC at Belfast, and inquired whether it was discretionary witb;the police to charge their guns with buckshot instead of ball. and to use their weapons without the previous reading of. the Riot Act ?—The Earl of CADOGA.N Was sorry to say the Government had a return of 28 deaths as having occurred during the lamentable disturbances in Belfast, but they had no means of ascertaining the exact number of wounded who had been admitted to the hospitals or who had been treated at their own homes. He, however, reminded his noble friend that a commission had been issued to inquire in- to the whole of the circumstances connected with the riots. The discretion in regard to the use of buckshot rested not with the police themselves but with the officers in com- mand, to whom was entrusted the duty of ordering with what charge the rifles should be loaded.—The motion was not pressed. The House adjourned at ten minutes to five o'clock until Monday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIMESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. ORDER Or SUPPLY.—The question put by Mr. Arthur O'Connor to the Coancellor of the Exclrequn as to the order in which supply will be proceeded with indicates that we are at last within measurable distance of the commence- ment of the real work of the session. Lord Randolph Churchill informed him that the army estimates would be taken first, and that these would be followed by the navy estimates and the civil service estimates in the order named. THE DEEATE.—LIVELY SCENE.

- _ There were upwards of sixty questions on the paper, and, 1 when they were disposed of, Mr. Peter M`Donald, in resum- log the debate on Mr. Sexton's amendment, earned the die- tinction of delivering the dullest and ,dreariest speech ever delivered within the walls of Parliament. Colonel SAIINDEaSON came to the rescue, and in his usual lively vein repeated the old sentiment which had drawn ringing cheers from an audience of Orangemen in Ulster that if the British Parliament imposed a Home Rule Parliament upon Ulster the rcen of that province would resist it by force. la the course of his harangue he had used very strong language—spoke of a blood-stained legacy of Mr. Gladstone's Adreinistration being tracked with blood, de- clared that Ulstermen neyer would go under the adnainistra- , tion ef jail birds, of men paid by foreign money, and then his etztravagance culminated in repeating the sentence about the determination of the Ulstermen to resist a Home Rule act by force. The Speaker called him to order not for the extravagance of his language, but for going beyond the question, and Colonel Saundersen, with some degree of pertness, replied," I am quite aware of that, sir." The Speaker got a little angry, and told him to adhere to his amendment, but Mr. Sexton would not allow the incident to terminate here, and asked if the honourable member warvia order in stating that he would openly by force resist any bill passed by Parliament. The Speaker's ruling was almost inaudible, but he did not rule Colonel Saunderson out of order, and apparently did not rule him to be be order either, for Sir William Harcourt got up and said it was of the tamost importance to have the Speaker's deci- sion on the language. Lord Randolph Churchill attempted to throw his •shield over thoXlsterman by asking if it was not ales usual to move that words objected to should be taken down. The Speaker again spoke in a low tone of voice, and left the matter much where it was ; but Lord Randolph Churchill intervened in a more effectual manner by writing a note and handing it to Major Waring, who looked at the addres and passed it on to Colonel Saunder- son, who had once more resumed his speech. The result of this note was that Colonel Saunderson's motion camf. to an untimely and preciDitate,end. Air. J. Morley then rose and vindicated himself against the charge which had been made against him of demoralising the police, and speaking disrespectfully of the Protestants of Ulster. The drift of the' Home :Rule policy, he said, was to heal the dissension of conflicting parties in Ireland, and not to foment it. This noble and elegant peroratien produced a loud ,cheer from the Home Rule benches. The debate was continued:by Colonel Waring, Mr. Clancy, Sir J. Corry, and Mr. 11. Campbell. At a late hour Mr. W. Redmond !joined in the debate, and came repeatedly into collision with the Speaker, who directed him to apologise to the House for characterising the remarks of other mem- bers as ungentlemanly.-4-On a division, Mr. Sexton's amend- , cnent was rejected LI, :225 to 123 votes. The singular circumstance that neither of the occu- pants of the trap nor the lads at the gates saw or heard the approaching train is accounted for by the character of the locality. The railway on the War- rington side of the crossing, that is the side on which the train was coming, forms a rather sharp turn about a hundred yards away, and this of course pre- vents a train from being seen at any distance, and the road from Mr. Grinishaw's house to the crossing lies lower than the railway, and is flanked on both sides with rather high and thick hedges, which hinder any one going along the road from seeing either up or down the line, while the gates of the crossing open outwards, and consequently the lads who held them open were also unable to see along the line because of the hedges. The dangerous character of this crossing is shown by the fact that three other fatal accidents are spoken of by residents in the neighbourhood as haying taken place within their experience. The deceased man Johnson, it may be mentioned, was thirty-one years of age, and lived in Price- street. He leaves a wife and two young children. He had been in the employ of Messrs. Smith and Milling for about seven years, and was a steady man and well thought of by his employers. The lad Willings is fourteen years of age, and lived with his parents in Greenall-street. THE INQUEST. The inquest as to the death of deceased was opened on Tuesday afternoon by Mr. S. Brighouse, at the public-house of Mr. Roughley, which is close to the scene of the accident. The solicitors present were Mr. T. J. Ridway, who appeared on be- half of Messrs. Milling and Co. and the relatives of the deceased; Mr. W. H. Jenkins, who represented Mr. B. Grimshaw, whose farm the deceased was returning from when he met with his death; and Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors' department of the London and North-Western Railway Company, Lime- street. The Coroner, in opening the inquiry, briefly re- capitulated the circumstances of the disaster, after which Martha Johnson, the wife of the deceased, was called as a witness. She said her husband and her lived at 37, Price-street. Ile was 31 years of age on his last birthday. She last saw him alive at half- past ten o'clock on Saturday morning, when he was well and in good health. She saw him dead on Sunday morning. Mary Walker, wife of Benjamin Walker, living in Gatewarth-street, the street which leads to the crossing, said she recollected deceased and another driving past her house in a trap on Saturday after- noon in the direction of Mr. Grimshaw's farm. At the time both the gates at the crossing were closed, and she unlatched the first gate for a little lad named Henry Crack, who pushed it open. The other gate was also opened before deceased attempted to cross the line to the farmhouse. The gates were then closed, ane.l she then went into her house. Metropolitan Undergreund Railway. Owing to a mishap in signallinn. a Great Western Company's Uxbridge train, when near Moorgate-street, broke the points and blocked the main line of the Metropolitan Railway. Several hundred passengers, carrying their luggage, had to alight in the tun- ael, and several thousand intending passengers for seaside resorts were unable to proceed, owing to the blocking of the line. ALARMING ACCIDENT TO A MANCHESTER EXPRESS. On Thursday evening an accident occurred at Penistone te the 8-53 p.m. (dining saloon) express from Sheffield to Manchester. The Huddersfield carriage had been detached, and in backing the engine to the train again the carriages were by some mishap forced backwards. Considerable damage was done to the roiling stcck, the brake being rendered unable to be taken forward, and a coal waggon, standing in the siding, against which it collided, greatly smashed. Many of the roof lamps were broken. about twenty passengers were hurt, and some of them were. brought on to Manchester. SCULLING CHAMPIONSHIP.—The final contest in the in' ternational sculling sweepstakes was decided on Wednes- day on the Thames championship course from Putney to Mc rtlake, the competitors being William Beach, Sydney, the champion of the world, and John Teemer, of St. Louis, United States. Beach e-ot off best, but Teemer was level at the end of half a mile. Directly afterwards Beach began to draw away, and at the mile was leading by a little over a length. He gradually increased his lead until at Ham- mersmith he was lengths ahead, and won as he liked. Beach took the first prize of £1,200, and retains the champion- ship. THE NEW SPANISH TREATY.—WhiIe this treater is sure to bring about an increased demand on the part of Spain for British manufactured goods, it provides also that all wines up to 30 degrees of strength shell be admitted into the United Kingdom at a duty of Is leer gallon. Enormous stocks of fine wines have accumulated in Spain, the remit of favourable vlutages, and a large increase in the consump- tion of Spanish wines may therefore be confidently looked for, resulting probably in Sherry once again becoming one of the favourite wines of this country. Our wine merchants here evidently share this anticipation ; indeed we notice that one house—Messrs. W. & A. Gilbey—are now offering to the public pert and sherry at is a bottle, both of which they guarantee to be pure foreign wines; while they quote the "finest and oldest sherry which Spain produces" at 3s 6d per bottle. If this can be done the Spataish Treaty is not without interest to the wine consumer.—The 21forning Post, August 26th, 18S6. HORRIBLE OUTRAGE AT BOLTON.—At Bolton, on Seturn day night, John Macdonald, labourer, returned to his home in Livingstone-street, in a cab about ten o'clock, apparently sober. Finding his wife outside the building, he dragged her by the hair into the house and assaulted her. She escaped by the back door, but it is said she was again . dragged into the kitchen, and Macdonald having locked the doors and drawn down the blinds he knocked her upon the floor and commenced to jump upon her head and body, be- sides hacking at her with a knife or chisel. The woman's screams brought neighbours to the rescue, but not before Mrs. Macdonald had received fearful wounds upon the head, while her right jaw was brotsen, several ribs were frac- tured, one of her breasts severely lacerated.• and her body was a mass of bruises. Macdonald is still at large. In 1879 he was committed at the Manchester Assizes to 15 years' penal servitude for having battered his wife's head with a ipoker and thrown her down some steps, but the sentence was reduced to a term of seven years owing to represents.- tions being made to the Home Secretary. A DIVE FROM BROOKLYN BRIDGE.—A printer named I Donovan dropped from the centre of Brooklyn bridge, /new York, on Sunday morning, striking the water squarely with his feet. He came up soon and swam towards the shore, near which he was helped into a boat by his friends who, were watching him. He was somewhat exhausted, but unin- jured. Donovan bad prepared himself for the leap by bendag- ing his legs and loading the soles of his canvas shoes heavily with lead in order that his feet might strike the water first. He and his companions rode upon the bridge in a waggon in order to escape the notice of the police. The.latter did not discern Donovan's purpose till they saw him serimmirg, and arrested him when be landed. The jump was made on a wager of five hundred dollars, and the distance peas nearly a hundred and forty feet. Donovan said afterwards, " When I let go the sensation was queer, and lasted pretty long. , Just before I struck water I felt myself swaying a little. Still I got there feet first and with my legs pretty close to- g• ether Of course, when I got under water the motion was a good deal slower, but still I went den-n at a great rate. I began striking out with my arms as soon as I could, and wasn't very long before I came to the surface. I felt all right, although there was a tingling sensation all over me."
