WE are beginning to. get at something like • the truth with regard to the war in Btu-210- h is corning to be looked upon as a much more serious matter than was originally an- ticipated; and both Mr.. S. SMITH and Mr. CREME:44 have rendered good service by calling the attention. of Parliament to the facts o'.'s the case. Mr. SMITH, on Monday evening, moved an amendment to the Ad- dress with the object of showing that it was unjust to burden lndiaa with the whole of the expenses of the war.-;: while Mr. CratmEn's amenglment went the leaszth of condemning the whole policy of the war. From the. speealaes that were made, and from the, voting that followed,,it is pretty evident that a considerable number of the members of the House of Commohs were in favour of both, amendments. It. will be remembered that .tha deposition of King THEEBA-CY and the, annexation of Bnrmah were announced when, Lard SALIssuRY.-was previously in, office, and: whilst Lord RA3DOLPIII Churchill was Secre- tary for India. It was, for a time, a sort of feather in the aap of his lordship; and it is not to be denied that the annexation was popular with the people of this country. The tyranny and cruelty of King T3ERBAW were ;of the most revolting kind; there was great discontent irahe country, and the idea had :.got abroad that if we did not move, and more 'quickly, France would, for trade purposes, 'step in and, take possession.. It semed in- evitable that there should be a grab at Bur- mah, and it was natural for England tos like her own grabbing better than that of Rance. Let US do Lord buEEEnaN, as Viceroy of India, the justice to say that he took some trouble to ascertain whether annexation would be an easy thing, and, whether there was reason to believe that it would on the whole be preferable to a Proteetorate. Ha came to the conclusion that annexation would be the best course to take, and he was allowed to act accordingly. There was very little diffi- culty in dealing with. the Kfrig ; the difficulty —and it is the usual difficulty in these cases —is with the people. 111-gaizerned and. wretched as in some respects the, Burmese are. they have no desire to be placed under a foreign yoke; there is such a thing as national sentiment amongst them, and they are at present giving expression to it by armed resistance. It is. a matter of course that, on account of the disturbed state of the country, there should be large bands of dacoits or bandits; bat beyond these cut-throats there is organised opposition. which is being vigorously directed by native princes. It is • no use shutting our eyes to the facts; it was said that taking possession of Bur- mah would be merely a military pro- menade; but reinforcements have had to be sent again and again; and the Under-Secre- tary for India admits that as soon as the cold season sets in it will be necessary to bring uP the invading forCe to 30,000 men—that is large an army as the French had in the Wax with Tonquin. We were very severe upon our neighbours for making war upon the Tonquinese ; but shall we at this moment look any better in their eyes through the annexation of Burmah by force of aims? The original es- timate for the expedition was £300,000; but that sum has already been swallowed uP many times over, and Mr. SAMUEL SMITH thinks it not unlikely that the war will cOSt us before it iS brought to an end from fiFe

millions to ten million: ot money. Looked at, as many have been disposed to regard it, as a commercial speculation, it must be ad- mitted that it is a ruinously bad transaction ; but it was the commercial men of this coun- try rather than of India who supported the policy of annexation; and it is extremely hard, now that the undertaking has turned out bad- ly, to call upon India to pay the piper. Mr. Small strongly objects to this course, and he had an easy task in showing that it was unjust and in politic. India is far poorer than any country of Europe; and the figures he quoted in support of his statement are simply appal- ling. Mr. SMITH said:— The average annual income of t,lle people of India was estimated by the most competent authorities at £2 per head, as against £33 per head in England. The whole income of the 200,000,000 of India was only one third of the income of the 36.000,000 of England. The yield from income-tax was only about one-tenth of what it was in this country, and when we remembered the population was six times as large we saw at a glance that upon any given area of population the income-tax paying power was only one-sixteenth of what it was in the Uni- ted Kingdom. Only one person in 700 reached an income of £5O a year. There were 50,000,000 who ate only one meal a day, and that meal of the very coarsest food. The great bulk of the peasanty were hopelessly in debt to the money-lender. Between 1870 and 1880 official statistics showed that 10,000,000 people died of famine. It is argued that India, poor as she is, ought to pay the costs of the war in Burmah, be- cause it was an undertaking for the protection of British. Burmah, and of our Indian do- minions in general ; but it is doubtful if the natives of India will see the matter in the same light. They will be disposed to con- clude that they are no better off, but rather the worse, for having to pay several millions of money, and at the same time have a dis- affected people on their borders. As Hr. CREMER aptly put it, let those who make the quarrel .be the men to Pay. British mer- chants were eager for annexation because they thought it would be good for British trade ; it was a commercial undertaking in their eyes, and, as it is proving disastrous they ought, at the very least, to bear a share of the loss. It may be that, when annexation was decided on, the road looked tolerably clear ; but it is certain that the matter was not one upon which the people of India were consulted. Indeed, Sir GEORGE CAMPBELL states that the grave step was taken without consulting the Council of India ; and if that be so it would appear that we have annexed in haste to repent at leisure. True, there is not much sign of repentance as yet ; 'that may come later on. Meantime, it is as well that the mind of the public should be direc- ted to what is going on in Burmah. We are putting down a rebellion—they are rebels, of course, even when fighting for their own country, who take up arms against the British Crown—and we are putting down that rebellion in the interests of the British Empire, And at the cost of British India ! We are a great people ; we display great qualities ; and amongst them, it seems, is great meanness.

THERE was nothing of special moment ' done at the half-yearly meeting, on Tuesday, of the shareholders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company; but the report presented by the Directors, and the speeches of the Chairman and of others interested in the project, show that preparations are being made for an extraordinary effort to raise the capital required. It is fully recognised, after the failure of Messrs. ROTHSCHILD to float the scheme, that, as Sir JOSEPH LEE said, they must trust less to the gods of finance and more to their own exertions. With a 'view to influencing public opinion, and put- ting the undertaking thoroughly on its merits. what may be called an outside Consultative Committee has been formed, with instructions to make the fullest inquiry into the scheme, the obtaining of capital, and the prospects generally of the company. It is. felt that an .expression of independent opinion will be more likely to influence investors than the statements of directors who are committed to the project. There can be no doubt that 'there is plenty of money in the country which is practically lying idle. What is required is to convince those who possP.ss it that it will be safe and profitable to invest in shares in the Ship Canal Company. But how is this to be done? There can be no question that Messrs. ROTHSCHILD'S failure to raise the capital had a depressing effect on what may be called the Ship Canal market, but that has passed off by the process of reaction. The public mind may now be said to be in a normal condition; and, if it can be quickly and strongly influenced in favour of the scheme, it is highly probable that the whole of the sum needed will be subscribed in due time. To this end there must be deeds as well as words; there has been no little en- thusiasm shown in Manchester, Warrington, and other places ; but the capitalists with money to invest naturally wants to know whether this enthusiasm pro- ceeds from those who are putting money in the undertaking, or whether it is a trades- men's and labourers' outburst at the prospect of getting money out. If the latter, he may think it intelligible, but not wholly encouraging; if the former, he has a right to ask that it shall be backed by a large demand for shares. It domes to this, that the outside public will not be likely t 9 stir until they see that in this. part of the country those who know most of the project are prepared to find a fair propDr- tion of the capital—say. from two to three millions. If this be done, we have no tear as to the rest of the money being forthcom- ing, and until it be done the directors are water-logged. It is satisfactory to see that they realise their position ; and that, what- ever else may be done in floating the scheme, there are to be no more leaps in the dark.

THE socking accident, on Saturday, at the level crossing at Sankey Bridges, by which one min lost his life and the youth who was with him was brought to death's door, has naturally exbited a considerable amount of attention in Warrington. It would be premature, whilst an inquiry into the circumstances is still pending, to express an opinion as to how .far blame attaches to anyone, or, for that matter, to indicate what steps should be taken to reduce to a minimum the chances of accident in tfie future; but we may express Our hearty approval of the sug- gestion of the Foreman of the Jury that the Board of Trade should be communicated ; with, so that the Government may be repre- sented when the inquiry is resumed. It may be that the Railway Company have done all that the law required of them in making pro- vision for the safety of the crossing but on the other hand it may blecome a question whether the law itself requites altering. It cannot be expected that Railway Companies will put someone in charge of crossings lead- ing merely to occupation roads; but when four lives have been sacrificed at one particu- lar spot, common sense and common humanity demand that something shall be done to more effectively fence off this particular death

trap. The crossing is obviously a dangerous one; it is near a sharp curve on the railway' ; the occupation road is below the level of the line ; and there is a thick-set hedge in the way. It is of moment, we may add, to know why the locks on the gates were not in use : and why Mr. GRIMSHAW, the farmer, said 'She did not think it would be safe for him to have the keys." The inquiry, we need hardly say, should be of the most searching kind; property has its value, but human life is in- valuable.

- TOUCH AND GO." Last night Lora Randolph Churchill pro- mised. to afford a special sitting, before the session closed, to consider a bill on the land question, which Mr. Parnell is prepared to lay before the House of Comrnons. What next?

The Newton Horticultural Society is to be congratulated on its first show ; it was a great success. Beautiful flowers are just as easily cultivated as ugly habits, but with what ; a difference in the result.

The Warrington School of Art re-opens on Tw)sday next, when, it is hoped, there will be a full attendance of eager and diligent stu- dents. Having secured a gold medal, and so many third-grade prizes during the past year,. the School has every encouragement to seek to obtain additional laurels.

Charles Cross, of Frodsham, has been fined 45s and costs for being in unlawful possession of game. He was found in possession of a hamper which contained 4.1 rabbits. Charles's explanation was that " he had found them in his back yard that morning." Our P. D. says he has looked in a back yard every morning since, but he has not yet been " hampered " in this way.

The Lymm Local Board have been penny wise and pound foolish in the matter of bye- laws. For years back the clerk has called attention to the need for a new set, and the Local Government Board have also dii ected attention to the matter. One member says that in some respects Lymm is in "a scanda- lous state ;" so by way of a remedy the Board have resolved, without further delay, to ad- dress themselves to the bye-laws question.

A man named Duffy has been fined 405. and costs at Widnes for breaking a land- lady's nose! The Chairman of the Bench said "they were much inclined to commit the defendant to gaol without the option of a fine." It is a pity they didn't do so. Such a fine under the circumstances is ridiculous. The Widnes magistrates do not set a sufficient value upon the nasal organ. " Forty shillings and costs" for breaking a woman's nose It is really setting a premium on the perform- ance.

Lord Randolph Churchill is not entirely happy. He has just intimated that he must decline for the present to attend public meet- ings. It is no wonder he finds his position a " hard and anxious" one. The man who climbs to the top of the tree from the backs of his friends, and gives them a kick at part- ing, must not expect to have an easy time of it.

Lord Lymington says it is idle and ridicu- lous to suppose that the Liberal Unionists are going to.play into the hands of the Glad- stone party; but what does he want? Does he suppose it would be less ridiculous for the majority to play into the hands of the mino- rity? Liberals of the Lvmington type may loiter on the road, 'but the party of progress must go forward; it cannot go back.

The Liberals of St. Helens are showing themselves alive and active by opening a Liberal club in Sutton; and the Liberals of Run- corn have come to the conclusion to move in the same direction. Nobody doubts that there is a Liberal majority in both these places; but the party requires keeping together, and educating in each political question as it arises. As the nights lengthen, some plea- sant and profitable hours may be spent in debate. Liberals have everything to gain by the spread of knowledge.

Russia cuts a wretched figure in connec- tion with the revolution and counter revolu- tion in Bulgaria. The " bear " wants to have his paw on the Balkan states; they are in the ditection of Constantinople. If the Rulers of these countries are wise, they will cease to show petty jealousy of each other, and combine for mutual protection. Single- handed, they will have no chance with Rus- aia ; united, they will be able to hold their own, and that is all they want.

Prince Alexander has tried the effects of submission; and the Czar has replied in a tone of studied insolence. If the Prince must go down, we would rather see him driven under .whilst struggling against fear- ful odds. His appeal to the Emperor of Russia is too humble; and the reply—well, it is that of a brute. What of the people of Bulgaria? Have they no voice in the question of who shall rule over them? They are stronger than Czars or Emperors, if they will but assert themselves, and be true to each other.

The Stockport Guardians have done a sen- sible thing. At a meeting on Monday, the House Committee recommended the Board to discontinue the allowance of beer to all officials, giving them one shilling each per week instead, the "porter and porteress to be allowed milk as usual," To be consistent, they should have gone astep further and con- verted the milk supply into cash. " Allow- ance " in the shape of liquor is an old bad institution. Pay a man properly for his ser- vices, whether at the workhouse or work- shop, and let him buy what he likes.

_ A RUNCORN MAN KILLED AT BIRKEN.HEAD. On Thursday a terrific explosion occurred at the inner entrance to the East Float at Birkenhead Docks. The steam tug Seagull, of Seacombe, of which Captain Reece, of Runcorn, was captain, was blown to atoms. The captain was seen shooting skywards to a bight of 60 feet, and his mangled body was found a few yards from where the stea- mer had been moored. Atough frightfully in- jured Captain Reece. was alive, but expired in the hospital half an hour afterwards. Two other men were also killed. . . THE DIVISION.—The minority supporting Mr. Parnell's amendment to the Address was composed of 103 Gladstonian LibeTals, including nine members ,of the late Government, one Unionist Liberal (Sir I Thomas Grove), and 79 Nationalists. The majority was made up of 260 Conservatives and 46 Unionist Liberals. The minority included Messrs. Jacob Bright, Potter, Schwann, J. Williamson, and Wright. In the majority were Messrs. Addison, A. J. Balfour, and Blundell, Colonel Bridgeman, Mr. Coddington, Lord Cranborne, Messrs. Shepherd-Cross, Edwardes- Moss, General Feilden, Sir J. Fergusson, Messrs. Forwood and Hardcastle, Lord Hartington, Messrs. Hermon - Hodge, Hornby, Howorth, Jennings, Knowles, Leake, Maclean, Maclure, and Powell, Sir M. White Ridley,.Colonel Sandys, Messrs. Seton-Karr, T. 11. Sidebottom, and •Tomlinson. Tn BEST PLACE for GROCERIES is at LAWLESS BROS., Market-place, Warriugton.—Advt.

MISDEMEANOURS AT WHISTON WORKHOUSE. For ab- litCOndilig from Whiston Workhouse. on the Ist iris'., before he was entitled to be discharged, John McNamara, A vag- rant, was senteßced by the Widnes magistrates. on Thurs- day, to 14 days' bard labour.—At the same court Tuotn,s La.sfin, a convicted thief, was charged witht stealing a pair of trnusers, a pair of boots, and a pair of braces from the Whiston Workkouse, on the 27r1i August. Mr. Williams, a porter. proved the case, and the prisoner WAS sentenced to three months' imprisonment with hard labour. THE ACTOR AND THE BILLPOSTER AT RUNCORN.—Thos. Benjamin Butler, an actor, appeared at the Runc,rn Police Court. on Monday, to answer a summons charging him , with assaulting David 6hepherd, billposter, Alcock-street, It was alleged that on the 13th August Saepherd was post- ing some bills at the Theatre Royal, when the defendant Caine up cud inquired who gave him orders to post bills there. He replied Mr. Waldron, and sys proceeding: with his work when the defendant flung him down, and "gave him a good knocking about." tie ea.; still suffering from the effects of the assault —For the defence evidence was called to prove that Shepherd was covering over the de- fendant's bills, and the assault was denied. The defend- ant simply gave him a push. A fine of is, and costs lie 61, was ire posed. A WIDNES WIFE BEATER—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursthy, a " powder packer" named Joseph Harrison \MS charged with neglecting to maintain his wife.—From the statement of Mr. Knowles, who represented Mrs. Harrison, it apneared that the defendant had been in the court twice to answer charges of assaulting his wife. He had, when liv- ing.: at Birkennead, thrown his wife to the ground, jumped upon, and so ill-used her that her life had been endangered. Toe woman was of a very respectable fatuity. It was fur- ther alleged that the defendant, who could earn about Xfl 12s weekly, had fr“:iiiently left his childreu without food whilst he spent his money in drinkinse—Evidence was called to prove tee defendant's brutality to his wire—The defendant denierl that he earned the money stoed, and stated that all the trouble had been caused by his wife insisting upon hav- ing her mother at the house. He was quite willing to pro- vide his wife a home.—The Bench said it was evident the man could not live quietly with his wife, and an order WV. made 110,11 hitil to pay 10a per week towards her mainten- ance, and pay the costs of that action, Including an advo- cate's fee of 10, 6d

--- - WIDNES CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.— The weekly meeting of the Widnes branch of the e.E.T.S. was held in the National Schools, Waterloo-road on Thurs- day evening. The Rev. J. R. JOReS, BA, curate, presided, and delivered an interesting adddress, which was followed by songs by various gentlemen. THE HYDROPHOBIA AMONGST CATTLE. Another cow belonging to Messrs. J. and U. Percival, Parkside Farm, Aston, showed symptoms of tables on Saturday, after being bitten five weeks ti,o by a toad dog, under eircumstarici-s previously reported. The cow suffered great agony and had to be shot, making the fourth which has died on this farm from hydrophobia. FOUND DROWNED AT FARNWORTIL—The body of an old man named John Fletcher, residing at Farnworth, was On Monday morning found by a man named William Standish . In a pond near the Horns Inn, in the village. The body was get out and taken to the inn, where it now lies awaiting I an inquest. Deceased, it is stated, had been drinking heavily of late, and this is supposed te have deranged his mind, and resulted in his committing suicide. tie wail G.l years of age, and had only one arm. RusrcouN, WESTON AND HALTON WATEaWORES COM- PANY.—The adjourned half-yearly meeting of this company wad held on Monday afternoon at the Public Hall. Mr. W. Hayes twas in the chair, and there were also presser Messrs. E. TollMiDP, T. Banks, W. Whittaker, Jas. thaw, Jas. Collier, Peter Smith, arid W. Salkeldysecretary.—Messrs. E. Timmins and T. Bankes were re-appointed directors, and Mr. R. B. Toft was re-appointed auditor. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the business. qtFuratuar, OF a .s.aLvaTioNts.r.—The interment of Mrs Martha Herringsbaw, a member of the Salvation Army, took place on Thursday afternoon at the Runcorn Ceme- tery. The funeral was attended by the band of the Salva- tion Army and a number of members. The body was borne by several members of the army in scarlet uniform with bands of white ribbon round the arm. On the way to the cemetery the mourners sang hymns accompanied hv the band. At the graveside several hymns were sung', and a short addresl was delivered by the captain of the

corps. ACCIDENTS AT WIDNES.—On Tuesday afternoon a brick- setter named Lloyd Robineon, residing in Travis-street, Simm's Cross, was following his employment at the Lanca- shire Alkali and Sulphur Company's works, Ditton-road, when be was struck on the head by a falling derrick, owing to one of the guide ropes giving way, and severely hurt. He was taken to the hospital, where he now lies. He is progressing favourably. A man named Rigby, residing at 11, Milton-road, Wines, bad one of his feet severely scalded on Monday by falling into some boiling liquor at the Widnes Alkali Company's works, where he is employed. He was taken home, and medical aid summoned. SIMMS CROSS PRIMITIVE MhTHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES. —ln aia of the trust fund of this chapel, sermons were preached on Sunday morning and evening by the RA,. J. Causland, of Runcorn. There were fair congregations. On Monday evening a tea meeting was held, and was well attended. The tables were in charge of Mesdames Owen, J. M. Jones, Wharton, Adams, Rollasen, Sage, Butler, and Williams, and Misses Wiles, F. Wiles, Crawford, and Mc- Connachie. Subsequently a public meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. S. Robinson, and the Rev. J. Cans- land &livered an interesting lecture entitled " The abori- gines of Australia." The usual votes of thanks were passed. SUNDAY SCHOOL FESTIVAL, RUNCORN.—The annual fes• tival of the scholars of Nelson-street Sunday school took place on Monday. The scholars, to the number of 230, as- sembled at the school at half-past one, and having formed in processional order, they walked through the town accom- panied by the superintendents, Messrs. Joseph Bazley and Peter Pendleburv. The younger scholars rode in a lurrr lent by Mr. Fletcher. The afternoon was spent very pleasantly in a field at En gber Runcorn, lent by Mr. Acker. The scholars were presented with various prizes by a number of gentlemen. On returning to the school, the children partook of an excellent tea, provided free of cost. WOBSPEOPLES Excurstoat FROM RUNCoRN.—The men employed in the various departments at the Bridgewater Navigation Company's yard, Old Quay, have had their annual excursion. The men and their wives, to the number of 200, left Runcorn at half-past eight in two of the company's lighters, towed by the tag Ashton, and proceeded up the Wearer, the party reached Anderton at 12 o'clock. They partook of lunch in a specially erected tent, and then pro- ceeded to Witton Brook. Thence they walked to Marbury Hall, and had the privilege of entering the grounds and gardens. In the afternoon a large portion of the party visited the rock mines of Mr. W. Hayes, in which they were much interested. Runcorn was reached at nine o'clock at night, after spending a mast enjoyable day. RUNCORN (406TH) STARR-BCWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY. —Tne annual meeting of this society was held in Bethesda Schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr. T. Handley presided, and there was a fair attendance. The report and balance sheet, which have been noticed in our columns, were adopted. Messrs. W. Armstrong, W. Booth, and A. Riley, retiring directors, were reappointed, and Mr. Porey was ap- pointed in place of Mr. R. Foulkes. The auditors, Messrs. W. Brookes and J. Cunnah, were reappointed, and the secretars'a (Mr. W. Handley's) salary was fixed at the same amount as previously, £45 per annum. After the conchn. sion of the business the 32nd appropriation took place, with the result that Mr. W. Brookes, of Waterloo-road, is entitled to an advance of £2oo.for 121 years, free of interest. An , appropriation also took place in connection with the Second Runcorn Starr-Bowsett Society, and Mr. Peter Hindley. of Lord-stteet, held two shares under the number drawn, and is entitled to an advance of £2OO, free et interest. "Nov A LODGING-HOUSE."—At Runcorn Police Court, on. Monday, Fanny Bullen, a middle-aged woman residing in Back Cooper-street was charged with keeping an unregis- tered lodging-house.—Mr. W. H. Linaker prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Commissioners, and Mr. J. W. Knowles, of Widnes, defended.—James Percival, nuisance inspector, stated that he visited the house in company with Sergeant Neild about half-past one on the morning of the 25th August. There were four persons in the house who were not members of the defendant's family—two men and two women of immoral character. The house was not regis- tered as a lodging-hoase.—Mr. Knowles contended that the house was not a lodging-house within the meaning of the Act. He called the four persons whom the inspector found in the house, and they stated they had lived there several weeks and did not pay anything for their accommodation.— The Bench were of opinion the house was not a lodging. house. and dismissed the case. STRANGE SUICIDE AT WIDNES.—Mr. Samuel Brighouse, the connty coroner, on Tuesday evening held an inquest at Widnes Police Court, on the body of Frances Cook. The deceased, a young woman, 33 years of age, was the wife of a brick maker, named Adam Cook, who lives at 7, Gerrard. street. On Saturday afternoon she received her husband's wages, and later, on her way to the butcher's, she lost her purse containing the money. The amount was about 15s 2d. The loss "seemed to trouble her very much," and she threatened to drown herself. Her husband said " Never mind ! If you have lest the money we can live with the loss of it, we have the house ;" and also, accord- ing to the testimony of a witness, treated his wife kindly. Twica the woman started on her way to the canal, but was brought back by Ellen Twigg, a neighbour, to whom she laughed as though the matter were a joke. About ball-past seven Mary Carroll saw the deceased walking towards the canal, apparently much distressed. She was cryingand saving " God help me." Next morning her dead body was fOtlnd in the canal by a boy named Edward Moss.—A verdict of "Found drowned" was recorded.

THE— NEW LANCASHIRE PEERS. —Viscount Cross and Lord Stanley deferred the taking of their seats in the House of Lords until Thursday. The new peers, according to the customary form, entered the House separately, preceded by Admiral Sir James Drummond, Gentleman Usher of the .Black Rod, and Sir Albeit Woods, Garter King-at-arms, and ac- companied by their sponsors, and delivered to the Lord Chancellor their patents of nobility. Then, having taken the oath, they were conducted to the bench appointed to theii rank in the peerage, and exchanged salutations with the Lord Chancellor, with whom they afterwards shook hands. RABIES IN CHESHIRE.-011 Saturday another of the cows belonging to Messrs. J. and G. Percival, Parkside Farm, Aston, which were bitten by a mad dog five or six weeks ago, showed signs of rabies, and after suffering great agony had to be shot. This is the fourth which has died on this farm from hydrophobia.—At Daresbury Sessions, on Tueday, an order was applied for by Superintendent Hol- lingworth to compel persons to keep their dogs under proper control. In answer to the Bench, the superintendent said that there had been suspected cases of hydrophobia in that district and two dogs were then suffering from it. It was also mentioned that similar orders were in force in the Altrincham, Runcorn, and Knutsford divisions. The order asked for was then made to remain in force for two months.

A FARMER'S SON KILLED AT BITIITONWOOD.—A shocking fatality occurred on Monday at Burton- wood, whereby a young man, aged 20, named Thos. Southern, son of a farmer of that name, living at Winwick-with-llulme, lost his life. Deceased, who was well known in Warrington, had gone with a horse and cart to the farm of Mrs. Fairclough for a load of potatoes, and was afterwards found lying deai in a ditch bordering the road leading from the farm. There were no eye-witnesses of the disaster, but it was surmised from the marks on the road that the horse had become restiv or attempted to run away, with the result that one of the wheels of the cart went into the ditch, the cart thereupon up- setting and falling on. deceased. When found, a portion of the front wheel of the cart was pressing his neck against the side of the ditch, and he was dead. An inquest was subsequently held, and a verdict of "Accidental death "returned. PRINTING OF EVERY DESCRIPTION, executed by John S. IRON TRADE SUMMARY—There has not been a very perceptible change in the English iron market during the past week; but it may be said that the restriction of the output of pig iron has conduced to greater firmness in vices, although there is no in- crease in the demand. The pig iron market of the North of England has continued steady, and a fair amount of business has been done at from 295. 9d. to 30s. per ton prompt. At Newcastle No. 3 Cleve- land pig is selling at 325. to 325. 3d. The Glasgow warrant .market has again been quiet this week, and very little new business is doing. There are no visible prospects of the Scotch trade being likely to improve soon. On Wednesday closing sellers of warrants were 395. 4d. cash and 395. 6d. one month, buyers offering id. per ton less. The hematite pig iron trade of the North-West of England is more satisfactory than it has been for some weeks, or 'even months, past: The demand for pig iron has increased considerably, and the market all round is much stiffer.—lron. THE NEWTON ELECTION.—On Saturday evening the return to Disley of Mr. Thomas Woodhouse Legh, eldest son of Colonel W. J. Legh, of Lyme Hall, member for the Newton Division, was made the subject of rejoicing amongst the Conservatives. Mr. Legh and his wife were met at the station by a large crowd of members of the Disley Habitation of the Primrose League and Conservative Association, with a brass band, by whom the member was escorted to the square near the Ram's Head Hotel, where an enthusiastic reception was given.—Mr. J. P. Liddell congratulated Mr. Legh on his having ob- tained such a high position. —Mr. John Alsopp, on behalf of the Primrose League, read an address from the League, of Which Mr. Legh is ruling councillor. Mr. Legh, in reply, adverted to his return as being not so much the result of his own efforts as of the principles which animated the breasts of the long- headed, hard-headed, and common-sense men of Lancashire. Referring to the po,icy of the Govern- ment in regard to Ireland, Mr. Legh said it would certainly be carried out on the true lines of thorough justice, impartiality, and the best interests of that country. (Applause.) DARESBURY LICENSING SESSIONS.—The annual Brewster Sessions for the Daresbury Petty Sessional Division were held at the Court House, Daresbury, on Tuesday, the magistrates present being Messrs. Edward Greenall (in the chair), C. Broadbent, W. Long, J. Marson, J. C. Parr, and W. C. Jones.—Su- perintendent Hollingworth submitted his annual report with reference to the conduct of the licensed victuallers and beer retailers in the Runcorn divi- sion during the past year. There were 23 licensed victuallers, 2 beersellers, and .3 others who sold off the premises, total 28, which gave an average of 298 of the population to each license. One licensed victualler had been proceeded against during the year, and convicted, as compared with two pro- ceeded against and one convicted in 1885. No beer- seller had been proceeded against, while 47 persons had been convicted of drunkenness, as compared with 31 in 1885.—The Chairman considered that the report was very satisfactory.—ln answer to a; ques- tion put by the Magistrates' Clerk, the Superinten- dent explained that W. J. Potter, of the Stag Inn, Walton Inferior, .had been fined 20s and costs for keeping his house open during prohibited hours, on the 16th of May. The whole of the licenses were renewed.—The license of the Stag Inn, Walton In ferior, was transferred from Walter J. Potter to Thomas Maddock. LAWLESS BROS. Sell the. BEST 2s TEA in the town.— Market-place, Warrington.—Advt.

- _ BREAKING A WIDNES LANDLADY'S NQSE..—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Messrs. W. D. Holt and H. S. Hall, a middle-aged man. named Edward Duffy, who stated that he had worked for the Local Board for 14 years, was charged with assaulting Mrs. Tilley, landlady of the Rose and Crown Public house, and also with refusing to quit that hotel.—Mr. Knowles appeared for the complainant and stated that about two o'clock on Saturday the defendant was in the house and wanted to fight another man. Mrs. Tilley told him that such conduct was not allowed, and afterwards permitted him to stay on going into another room and promising to be quiet. An hour later he was en- gaged in a discussion on the Belfast riots, and was about to strike the man with whom he was disputing, when Mrs. Tilley, who knew theedefendant well, teok hold of his arm and said, " Come along Teddy," wishing to take him out of , the house. He then struck her on the nose with his fist and broke the upper part of the nasal bone. Mrs. Tilley had since suffered great pain, and Linn unable to attend to her household duties.—Superintendent Barker informed the Bench that the defendant was charged with assault in 1879, and was also charged with assaulting a man named Wilding on Saturday.—Wilding said he wished to withdraw the charge.—Mr. Holt said it was abominable that a woman, who was trying to keep a respectable house, should be as- saulted in this manner, and the magistrates wore much in- clined to commit the defendant to gaol without the option of a fine. For the assault the defendant was fined 40s and costs, 7s 63 ; and for refusing to quit 20s and costs. 12s, or, In default, two months' hard labour. FUNERAL OF MRS. ROBINSON.—The funeral of Mrs. Mary Martyn Robinson, widow of the late Rev. Wm. Robinson, who was the first pastor of Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn, took place on Thursday afternoon, in the burial ground attached to the Bethesda Chapel. The death of Mrs. Robinson, who was within a few days of the completion of her 77th year. occurred on Monday last at the residence of her step-son, Dr. Robinson, Belvedere. Mrs. Robinson's life has been distinguised by many acts of kindness, and her loss to many poor people will be keenly felt. The body was borne to Bethesda Chapel by way of Church-street, and the funeral was witnessed by large numbers of people who exhibited marks of profound respect. The bier was wreathed with ivy, and the coffin was covered with wreaths and flowers sent by Mrs. Beck, Mrs. Williams, Mrs. William Brookes, Mrs. and Miss Hartley, Miss Bankes, Miss Andrews. Mrs Harrison, Mrs Allen, Mrs S Mason, the Helsby cottagers, and other friends. The mourners were Dr. and Mrs Robinson, and their domestic servants. The body was preceded by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, Dr. McDonnell. Mr. Bankes, and Mr. Francis Beck, Mr. William Handley, Mr. Jos. Littler, Mr. John Williams, Mr. Thomason. and Mr. D. H. Jones. On arriving at the church the burial service was conducted by the Rev. J. D. Thomas. In the course of an address the rev, gentleman made feeling reference to the consistent attendance at the chapel by the deceased. Special hymns were sung by the choir in the chapel and at the graveside. Mr. John Ravens. croft presided at the organ in the chapel. The sides of the grave were covered with ivy, picked out with chrysanthe- mums, and the last solemn rights were conducted very im- pressively. Mr. D. H. Jones and Mr. J. Thomason had tcharge of the arrangements.

ing.—Mr. Dobson suitably replied, and in response to re- peated calls, Mr. Hankinsonlmade a speech. His sentiments were contained in his election addrees, and he could add

There was a considerable amount of stir in the usually quiet village of Penketh on Thursday, on the occasion of the marriage of Mr. Charles Edward Parker, of Home Lea, Penketh (manager at the Penketh Tanning Co's. Works), to Miss Helen Gar- nett, second daughter of Mr. Robert Garnett, of Ye Hall Nook, Penketh. Both the bride and bride- groom are well known and much respected in the village, the latter having taken an active interest in what may be termed the public affairs of the lo- cality, besides being president of the Penketh Liberal Association, while the bride has during the past three years held the office of honorary organist at the Wesleyan Chapel. During the day the Tan- ning Co's. works, and the cabinet-making establish- ment of Messrs. Garnett and Sons, and the Liberal Club were hung with flags in honour of the event. The marriage took place at the Wesleyan Chapel at noon, but an hour before that time there was a con- gregation in the place of worship which filled it to the door, many persons from Warrington attending. There was also a large gathering cutside the chapel door. On the bride entering the chapel on the arm of her father a select choir of school children sang the hymn " The voice that breathed o'er Eden," Mr. James Muir presiding at the organ. The bride was attired in cream satin merveilleux and moresque lace, with the usual orange blossom and veil, the dress having been made by Messrs. Woolwright, Liverpool. The bridesmaids were Miss Good (Hull), Miss Garnett, Miss F. Garnett, Miss Parker sister of the bridegroom'). Miss Moses. Miss A. Moses (cousins of the bride), and Miss Hilda Gar- nett, and they were each dressed in cream lace 'muslin, and carried a handsome bouquet of choice flowers. The groomsmen were Mr. W. Walker (Bolton), Mr. E. Parker, Mr. Gordon Parker, Mr. R. E. Garnett, Mr. W. Posnett, Mr. A. Davison, and Mr. P. C. Garnett. The officiating minister was the Rev. ' F. Payne, of Colwyn Bay, and formerly superinten- , dent in the Warrington Circuit. As the party left ,the chapel after the ceremony, Mr. Muir played Mendellsohn's "Wedding March." There were six carriages present, five of which were supplied by Mr. Connor, Sankey-street, Warrington, and the other was Mr. R. Garnett's private brougham, and in these the wedding party and guests were con- veyed to Ye Hall Nook. Here Mr. T. Birtles, photo- grapher, Warrington, was in attendance, and photo- graphed in front of the house the whole party, after which the bridal party and then the bride and bridegroom were separately taken. In the after- noon the bride and bridegroom left Penketh for Switzerland by way of London and Pari.s. We understand that on their return they will live at Vine House, Penketh, the residence of the late Mr. R. Garnett. The guests present were :—Mr. and Mrs Fildes (Stretford), Mr. and Mrs Cathcart Smith (Chester), Mr. and Mrs David Garnett, Mrs Jenks (London), Mr. and Mrs W. Par- ker (Dundee), Mr. and Mrs T. Walker (Bolton), Mr. and Mrs Davison (Darlington), Dr. and Mrs Hur- ter (Bold), Rev. F. Payne (Rhyl), Mrs Do. lg (Car- lisle), Miss James (Carlisle), Mr. Corwen Miss Raper (London), Mrs and Miss Longbottom (Bowdon) Mr. Robert Posnet (Penketh), Mr. Charles David- son (Penketh), and Mr. John Gornall (Penketh).. On Monday, the workmen connected with the tannery, presented the bridegroom. Mr. Parker, with a valuable timepiece on the occasion of his marriage. The men having assembled Mr. Randall, the foreman, addressing Mr. Parker, said "Mr. Par- ker, on behalf of the workmen here,l beg to present you with this timepiece as a mark of their esteem and respect, and in doing so we wish yourself and future wife long lite and every happiness."—Mr. Parker, in thanking them, said 'he felt quite taken by surprise—but he did feel deeply grateful for the kindness and good feeling which had prompted them to give expression to the warm feeling of re- gard they had always shown towards him, and on behalf of himself and his 'intended wife he warmly thanked them. Ile perceived the timepiece was a very valuable one, but lie estimated it as an expres- sion of their affection and esteem. He had the utmost confidence in the workpeopie that they would still show the same interest in the working of the con- cern as they had done in the past. The pleasant relations between them had never been broken since the tannery was started. He hoped that on his return there would be a social gathering, when he could more fully speak on subjects of mutual interest. He then intimated that they were all welcome to be present at the the marriage pn Thursday, and have a holiday for the rest. of the day, which he hoped they would en- joy. We may add that the timepiece, which will g 6 for 400 days, was supplied by Mr. Carter,. of Bridge-street, Il arrington. It bears the following inscription on silver :—" Presented to Mr. C. E. Parker by the employes of the .Penketh Tanning Company on the occasion of his marriage. Sep- tember 2nd, 1886." On Wednesday Mr. Parker and Miss 11. Garnett were presented with a silver epergne by Mr. James

THE SANITARY CONDITION OF WIDNES— GOVERN:VIENT INSPECTION. Yesterday afternoon a special mee .ing of Widnes Local Board was held for the purpose of hearing a report on the sanitary condition of Widnes by Dr. Page, a Local Govern- ment Board inspector. Dr. O'Keeffe presided, and there Were present besides Dr. Page, Messrs. D. Wright, J. Mid- wood, H. Cook, F. Haves, J. Houghton, J. T. Allen (clerk), Higginson (surveyor), Dr. Cooper (medical officer of health), and Dickson (nuisance inspector.)—Dr. Page ex- plained that he was there by the instructions of the Local Government Board, and had during the last week carried out an inspection of the Urban Sanitary district of Widnes in connection with the general survey of the sani- tary district which the Local Government Board had during the last two years ordered on account of the prevalence of cholera and the possibility of the introduction of that disease into this country. The object of the survey was to enable the Local Government Board on the one band, and the Sanitary Authority on the other to consider the sanitary requirements of the district, and to place at disposal of the Sanitary Authority the necessarily large experience which the Local Government Board had of saeltary matters and remedies. He was well aware of the difficulty under which the Widnes Local Board was placed in regard to their work. They had a somewhat exceptional population to deal with on account of the peculiar industries which constituted the staple trade of Widnes, but, notwithstand- ing many difficulties, they had given great atteation to water supply, which he was glad to have to speak of in very favourable terms. They had also given attention to works of main sewerage and improvement of streets, and had taken a decided leap in advance of many sanitary authorities in coming to the conclusion to provide the district with the necessary provision in cases of infectious disease. The plan they had adopted for this was a very good one. His object, however, was to call their attention to the sanitary short- comings which the inspection had brought to light, and the best means of dealing with them. With respect- to the dispesal of excrement and house refuse, the nuisance from midden privies, close to dwelling houvs, frequently against dwelling-houses, was considerable, owing to defective con- struction, allywing of excessive accumulation. The manner in which excremental refuse was removed was inefficient, and was not very satisfactory, and gave rise to complaints which ought not to exist. An unpleasant and unwholesome state of houses arose from a want of proper paving and channelling of yards, and the gullies in many cases were dilapidated. Generally the yards were in a very di-ty and neglected state. In some small yards there were animals kept in all sorts of sheds, and the air space there should be there for the preservation of health. was crowded out with such things. This was a state of affairs that should not exist. The private streets and back passages in nearly every instance showed general neglect. There was a want of scavenging, and they were littered with refuse and ashes. These showed a state of things which was the very opposite of what the streets adopted by the Board showed. The ventilation of sewers was in need of improvement. In many of the streets, especially private streets, there were no ventilators of any kind, and it was desirable that the whole of tha sewers should be yentilated.—The Clerk pointed out that the Board had no power over private streets.—Dr. Page said main sewers and approach sewers should be ventilated at intervals of not more than 100 yards. House drainage ought to have the means of free ventilation too. It was desirable also that there should be a system of flushing at frt qtvnt intervals during the year of the whole of the sewers. He referred to the unsatisfac- tory state of Farnworth sewerage, and said the sewerage of Appleton was likely to be improved and diverted from its pre- sent course when the main sewer was extended. Bowers Broek was very unsatisfactory, and the nui9ancee arising therefrom were not pleasant to the houses in the neighbourhood. It

Watson, on behalf of the teachers and scholars of the Wesleyan school, Penketh. The presentation was made at the school, Mr. Parker and Miss Garnett being accompanied by a few friends. The teachers present besides the head master, Mr. Watson, were Mrs. Wilson, Miss M. Ashton. Miss Maud Seed, Miss M. E. Mainley, Miss A. Dunabin, and Miss Rout— ledge.

The annual meeting of the Licensing Committee of the borough of Warrington was held at the Ses- sions-room, in Irlam-street, on Monday, for the purpose of hearing applications for fresh licenses. The magistrates on the Bench were Alderman Davies (in the ctiair), Alderman Holmes, Coun- cillor Greening, Dr. Gornall, Mr. F. Monks, Mr. D. Garnett, and Mr. E. J. Guest.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. P. Speakman. Present—Messrs. Dobson, Grice, Mellor, Meadowcroft, Lightburn, Taylor, Farrell, White, Pritchard, R. Shaw, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshell (secretary), Dr. McDougall (medical officer), and M. Barker (survsyor.)

, WoaxlN TiiE CommtrrEE.—On the recommendation of the Highway Committee the tender of Messrs. T. Kirkham and Company for flagging the footpath on the west side of Bridgewater-street, was accepted. The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the month amounted to £268 Os 7d, and accounts amounting to £l9B 9s id were passed for payment. It was decided on the recommendation of the Health Committee, that the nightsoil tipping wharf, situa- ted in Mill-street, be enclosed, and the gate thereto be kept I ()AA. TRH NUISANCE INSPF.CTOR.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the re-appoint- Ment of Mr. J. Percival as ingpector of nuisances. Goon BYE.—At the conclusion of toe business, the chairman asked if any member had anything to bring for- ward. Perhaps some of them might not Meet there again. (Laughter.)—Mr. Grice said while he had been a member of the Board he had always experienced great courtesy, and if he did not come again he should have very peasant memories of the Board.-Ir. Mellor Better say good bye and retire. (Laughter.)—There was no other busi- ness.

div.head: PETITIONS.
div.p: PETITIONS.

Before the business commenced the Rev. E. Moore asked permission to present a memorial to the Bench on the subject of the granting of new licenses. The petition, which was handed to the Bench, read as follows :—" To the Worshipful the magistrates of the borough of Warrington,—We, the undersigned clergy and ministers of the bor- ough of Warrington, beg to present this respectful memorial to the bench of magistrates this day sit- ting in Brewster Sessions. Believing that the houses licensed for the sale of intoxicating liquors within the borough which already exist, are amply sufficient for its requirements, we earnestly entreat the Bench not to grant any additional facilities for the sale of intoxicating liquors, which may be asked for at these sessions. The memorial was signed by the Revs. W. Quekett (rector), E. C. E. Carleton (Holy Trinity), S. Wilkinson (St. Paul's), M. Schonberg- (St. Peters), J. H. 4ones and G. E. Cutting (Wesleyan), J. Wernock (Presbyterian), John Yo.nge (VVycliffej, W. R. Parry (Cockhedge Mission), J. Allton (St. Barnabas), J. Calvert (Primi- tive Methodist), E. Moore. (Baptist), P. Slater (St. James's), J. Thompson, F. W.. Sumner, and J. F. Carew (Roman Catholic.)—Alderman Davies: You don t want the magistrates to grant any additional licenses. Does the memorial go so far as to sug- gest to the Bench that they should not entertain , any applications for the. *transfer of a license from • one side to another ?—The Rev. E. Moore replied that the prayer of the petition was that, believing the houses already licensed amply sufficient, they earnestly entreated the Bench not to grant any ad- ditional facilities.—The Rev. G. E. Cutting said that he had a similar memorial to present from the War- rington Band of Hope Union. He should like to place the memorial in the hands of the Bench with an earnest request that its prayer be heard on behalf of Warrington. The petition referred to was as fol- lows :—" To the worshipful the magistrates of the borough of Warrington assembled at the licensing sessions, 1886. The memorial of the undersigned officers of the Warrington Band of Hope Union respectfully sheweth, that it is the opinion of the Executive Committee of the said Union that no suf- ficient cause exists for any increase in the number of licensed houses for the sale of intoxicating drinks in this borough ; that, in the interests of the chil- dren and young people of the town, it is highly desirable to limit the sale of such drinks as much as. ; that, therefore, your memorialists earnestly desire that your worshipful bench may decide to decline any additional licenses that may be applied for. On behalf of the committee of the Warrington Band of Hope Union.—(Signed) R. A. Naylor, President; Wm. Roberts, Chairman of Committee; Joseph. Titchet, Treasurer; and Frank Williams, Secretary.
APPLICATIONS.

Mr. Robert Davies said that he thought he might say that he felt himself, and he was sure that from past experience he might add that the magistrates also felt, that the number of licensed houses in War- rington was not likely to be increased under any circumstances. His application that day was one of another character. It was put in the form of an application for a new provisional license for a house intended to be erected, but apart from that techni- cality, it was really an application to shut up four houses and to build one in their place. He thought that the magistrates must feel that many of the public-houses in Warrington were fit for nothing at all but for the purposes of drinking. The object of his clients, Messrs. Greenall and Company, was to give up some of these beerhouses, and to build houses similar to those which could be seen in the town, such as the Norton Arms, and the more, re- cently built Roebuck in Bridge-street. These houses had stabling and other accommodation. Ile might say, as he knew there was great misappre- hension on the subject, that his clients did not derive one penny piece from any of their houses through the sale of spirituous liquors therein. They confined themselves to the legitimate trade of brewers, and they did not care, so long as a house was respectable, whether it had a full license or not. The house in regard to which the application was made was proposed to be erected at the corner of Hoyle-street and Bewsey-road, and it was to meet a want much felt in the neighbourhood. Ile heard on all sides that there was an amount of out- door drinking over Bewsey bridge that it was very sad to contemplate, and which could not be for the good of the public morals. He thought that all would be of opinion that if a house was erected at the place alluded to, at an estimated cost of .£2,500, it would provide respectable accommodation, and was less likely to be used for drinking purposes than dens where people just went in and got a. . glass of beer and came out. There were legitimate purposes for which licensed houses were used. A great deal of business was obliged to be done in licensed houses, for which every accommodation was provided, and it was for this legitimate accom- modation that he was then applying: He was pre- pared, in return, to give up the Green Dragon public-house in Bridge-street, and three houses for the sale of beer which had off licences. He had not a word to say. disrespectful or otherwise, of the memorials. Alrfadmitted that a certain amount of abuse accompanied almost everything,, and he. con- tended that one way of doing away with the abuse of drinking facilities, was to get rid of some of the mere drinking shops and replace them with licensed houses. He remembered Mr. Peter Rylands, many years ago, when on the Bench, wishing that sonic power or other could properly distribute and weed down the licenses in Warrington. It had always been his (Mr. Davies's) argument that that should be done, that many of the old licenses should be done away with, and that respectable and larger houses, w.ith good accommodation, should take their places.—Mr. John Pierpomt, architect, then submitted plans of the proposed new building, and said that he had often noticed outdoor drinking in the neighbourhood of Bewsey. Mr. R. Davies then made a second application in regard to a house proposed to be erected in Batters- by-lane, a distance from any licensed premises. In this case Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company, were prepared to give up the White Bear beerhouse in Buttermarket-street, and the Sceptre Inn in Winwick-street. They were algo prepared to close , the Pelican full licensed house in Buttermarket- street, where there were so many clustered to- gether. The application was to accommodate the Orford end of the town. It was proposed to }mind stabling to this house also. Mr. Percy Davies applied for an extension of a license that had been granted for eleven years for the Grove, Bewsey-road. He represented Messrs. Wagstaffe and Company, of Manchester, a respect- able firm, who, unfortunately having no other houses in Warrington, had therefore no plum to offer in the shape of giving up other licenses in or- der that the Bench would see fit to grant the appli- cation. Eleven years ago the house was pnrchased for a large sum, and it was then supposed that there would be no difficultywhatever in getting the license granted. Mr. A. Browne made an application on behalf of Samuel Hartshorne, beerseller, Railway Tavern, Bank Quay. The property, he said, did not belong to any brewery, or firm, but 'to the holder of the license. He handed in a petition signed by 70 householders living in the immediate neighbour- hood.—Alderman Davies remarked that many of the signatures appeared to have been written by the same person.—Mr. Browne admitted that some of the people could not write, and their names had been written by one person. They were, however, legitimate. The nearest licensed houses were the Bowling Green, 316 yards away, and the Railway Inn, 400 yards distance. These were all the applications, and after a pri- vate consultation, the Bench declined to grant any of them.

The Severn Tunnel was opened on Wednesday with mineral traffic. Partridge shooting began on Wednesday, and in many parts substantial has were made. Considerable opposition is, it is said, likely to be mani- fested from the Radical and Yitionalist 13, rches to the reap- pointment of Mr. Courtney to the Chairmanship of Ways and Means. The Dissentient Liberals intend to conduct a vigorous campaign on their own account during the recees. A meet- ing of the party will shortly be held to discuss the arrange.. ments necessary for the work. .

POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON. BOROUGH COURT. MosmaY.—Before Alderman Davies (in the chair), Alder- man Holmes, Councillor Greening, Dr. Gornall, Mr. R. Garnett, Mr. F. Monks, and Mr. E. J. Guest. DRUNKENNESS &C.—John Loftus was fined 105 and costs for being drunk in Bewsey-rPad, on Saturday night, and for begging.-3rien McDonough was fined a like amount for being drunk and disorderly in the Market-place, on Satur- day nigtit.—John Rowland was fined 5s and costs for being -drank in Buttermarket-street, John Shields 105 and costs, and Mary Whalley 5s and costs for smilar offences.—Thos. Clegg was dismissed on a charge of being drunk in Bewsey- road.—Peter Clou4h, for being drunk on the platform of the Cheshire Lines Railway, was fined lOs and costs.—Ruihard Dun was fined 5s and costs, Mary Hughes 5s including costs, Elizabeth Spencer 5s including costs, Mary Quinn 5s in- cluding costs, and Elizabeth Fleming 5s and costs, on charges of drunkenness. DISTLHBING THE PELCE.—Charles Shepherd, Frederick Smith, John France, and George Bromley were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting on land off Bewsey-read, on the 21st August.—Shepherd was tined 51 I and costs for being drunk, and the others were ordered to ' find a surety to keep the peace. STONE-THROWING.—Two boys named William Deakin and George Thomas were ordered to be birched for stone- throwing in Arpley-street ; and Arthur 0. Clay was fined 2s 6d, and the costs of the summons, for throwing stones in Parker-street. PITCH AND Toss.—Martin Lyons and Thomas Oates were each sent to prison for fourteen days for playing at pitch and toss in Cloth Hall-yard, on the 23rd inst. A STR.A.Y lionsz.—Jaines Monks, for allowing a horse to stray in Bewserstreet, was ordered to pay 2s 6d, and the cost of the summons. Dzszirrtox.—Albert Taylor, a deserter from a regiment stationed at Windsor, was remanded for safe custotiv. A BAD CuanacrEn.—John Noon, charged as a had char- acter with frequenting the streets with intent to commit a felony, was sent to prison for a month THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. A DESEWIER.—CharIes Whittaker, a deserter from H. M. South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Pontefract, was remanded to Btrangeways to await an escort, SLEEPING °cr.—William McGowen was sent to prison for fourteen days for sleeping out in the coal yard of Fred. Massey, Tanner's-lane, the same morning, without visible means of subsistence. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, Dr. Gomall, and Mr. R. Garnett. A VIOLENT WOMAN.—Ann Dutton was charged with do- ing malicious damage by breaking a window at the Work- house, to the amount of is, on the Ist inst., and with assaulting James Curry, porter, at the same time and place. —Evidence was given to the effect that she threw stones at Curry, one of which broke a window, and Dr. Spinks said that she was more like a wild beast than a human being.— She was sent to prison for a month. VAGRANCY.—WiIIiam Read and Albert Furness were charged with sleeping in the brickfield of Messrs. Roberts and Looker. Bewsey-road. Mr. H. Roberts said that of late great damage had been done by trespassers on the brick- field. They were sent to prison for seven days. THREATS. Margaret Barlow, sum mooed for using threatening language to Mary Jane Monks,was ordered to be bound over for six months in her husband's recognisaaces a a.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WZDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Z. Armitage and J. Tinsley. DRUNK IN CHARGE OP A HORSE{ AND CART.—James Hudson, a youth, was summoned for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart at Rixton, on the 18th ult, and was fined 5s and costs. DRUNKRNWRSB.—A. fine of 5s and costs was imposed on Thomas McEvoy for being drunk at Great Sankey. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Jobn Corley, farmer, was summoned for assaulting his wife, Nancy, on the 18th August, at Rix- ton. Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. Fleming (barrister), instructed bv Messrs. Croft and Craven, of Manchester. for the defence.—Mr. Davies said that on the day in question Mrs. Corley was locked out of the house, but succeeded in effecting an entrance. Defend- ant took hold of her by the shoulder, and put her out of the house That was the assault complained of. Defendant bad only recently been before the Court for a similar as- sault, and was bound over in his own recognisance of £2O to keep the peace towards his wife. 1 he parties had been mar- ried something like 20 years, and bad seven children, and unsuccessful attempts had been made to effect an amicable arranvensent. Mrs. Corley now stated that she did not want to live apart from her husband, and desired to with- draw the charge. Def4ndant, however, declined to live with her.—Mr. Fleming said the defendant did nut use any vio- lence whilst ejecting his wife, and the law pro Tided that a husband could eject his wife if she was disorderly. He was anxious that the parties should come to an amicable arrangement.—The magistrates made an order to the effect that defendant should contribute 17s 6d towards the main- tenance of his wife, Ind directed that she should have the custody of the youngest child. VAGRANCY AT POULTON.—John McLean, Thomas Mahar, John Joseph Banningham, James Knight, William Lancely, Richard Hughes, and John Jones were charged with va- grancy by sleeping in a cornfield belonging to Mr. Bennett, at Poulton.—Defendants were discharged with a caution.

D&RESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. Edward Greenell, C. Broadbent, W. Long, J. Marson, J. C. Parr, and W. C. Jones. ASSAULT ON A YOUNG WOMAN.—Samuel Wright, a boy, was summoned for committing an assault upon a young woman named Annie Yarwood.—Mr. R dgway (of Warring- ton) appeared for the prosecution, and Mr Percy Davies (of Warrington) for the defence.—Defendant was fined 20s and cute, or one month's imprisonment. A 001V-EEEPER FlNED.—William Leech, a cow-keeper, pleaded guilty to carrying on his business without being registered, according to the requirements of the Act of Par- liament.—He was fined is and costs. Smoot, Cssus.—The following persons were fined 5s sash for not sending their children regilarly to school : John Hatton, David Jones, Wchard Hamblett, Thomas Harver, Edwin Ratcliffe, John Robinson, Charles Delooze, R. G. Williams, and George Lightfoot.—Mr. Da Prez proved the cases. A PunLicate FINIM.—Elirl Cooke, landlady of the Lon- don Bridge Inn, Appleton, was summoned for having sup- plied intoxicating liquors to a drunken person. named John Hardy, on the 24th of July. Hardy was summoned for being drunk on licensed premisee.—Mr. Robert Davie., of Warrington, appeared for the defence of Mrs Cooke.—P.C. 106 stated that about four o'clock in the afternoon of the day in question he saw Hardy in a trap with a man named Simpson. Hardy got out of the trap, and went into Mr. Cross's shop. He afterwards went to the Mulberry Tree inn; but as he was drunk the landlord refused to supply him with drink. Hardy again got into the trap, and went in the direction of the London Bridge Inn. Witnees went into the police station, which is close to, and afterwards proceeded to the inn, where he saw Hardy, who was drunk, with a glass of beer in his band. The ale was supplied by the daughter of Mrs Cooke, and on Mrs Cooke heing told about the offence she said she was very sorry, and admitted that Hardy was not sober.—Sergeant Booth gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. Robert Davies stated that there was no house in the divi- sion better conducted than the London Bridge Inn. He would advise Hardy not to get drunk in future, and go to respectable publican's houses to get them into trouble, as the constable had admitted that he had charged -Hardy with doieg in this case.—A married daughter of Mrs. Cooke stated that Hardy appeared to be sober when he was sup- plied with drink. She did not cry when the policeman spoke to her.—Charles Davenport also gave evidence for the defence, and positively swore that Hardy was sober a short time before he went into the London Bridge Inn.— Mark Cross, shoemaker, Stockton Heath, said Hardy called at his house between three and four o'clock on the after- noon in question. Hardy was a little fresh, but was not drunk.—Hardy stated that he had bad three glasses of beer at Warrington, and he had nothing else to drink.--The Bench were of opinion that the charge was proved, and fined Hardy 55 and costs for being drunk, and Mrs. Cook ci 5s and costs for supplying ale to Hardy, this being her first of- fence.

UNnerf SCALEIL—George Barlow, shopkeeper, of Walton Inferior, was summoned by Superintendent Hollingworth for being in possession of a pair of flour scales which were 11 drachms against the purchaser on the 18th August. Fined 5s and cests.—John Mos.. of Higher Walton„charged with being in the possession of two pairs of scales, one of which were against the purchas.r, and the other against himself, was also fined 5s and costs. CARELESS DRIVE.R,S.—John Pearsp, for riding on a lorry at Preston-on-the• Hill on the 27th July, without reins, was fined 2s 6d and costs.—John Carter, charged with being asleep whilst in charge of a horse and lorry at Daresbury, on the 18th August, was fined is and costs.—Thomas Walker, charged with a similar offence at Stretton, on the 24th July, was fined Is and C95t5. DRUNKENNESS—MichaeI Dowd, charged with being drunk and disorderly at Stretton on the 24th July, was Japed 78 61

and costs.—George Bate. charged with a similar offence at Grappenhall, was fined 103 and costs. ALLEGED THEFT FROM a TlLL.—James Portland and John Appleton were charged with having stolen 10., the moneys of Isaac Saunders, shopkeeper, of Whitley Infe- rior, on the 20th August.—Prisoners were remanded for a week to the warrington Occasional Court House. THEIr BY A SERYANT.—Emma Leech (14) WAS charged with having stolen a pair of boots and two yards of cello.. at Acton Grange, on the 23rd of August, the property of Peter Hall. Plisoner, it was stated, left the service of the prosecutor on the date named, after which it was discov- ered that the articles bad been taken. She was arrested at Pinner's-brow, Warrington, where she said she was very sorry for baying committed the robbery.—The prisoner's father said his daughter had given him trouble before, and had once attempted to commit suicide.—She was sent to gaol for 14 days, and was ordered to se afterwards detained in a reformatory for four years.

• WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. TOPERS.—A fine of 5s and costs, or seven days in default, was imposed upon each of the following persons for having been guilty of drunken conduct :—John Dagnall, John Tarleton Patrick Tarleton, John Traynor, John Hayes, Edward 'Hynan, George Morrow, Mary Cosgrove, Richard Kenwright, Thomas Healey, Robert Grace, Robert Lee, William Smith, and Patrick Spelman. CHanots or BURGLARY.—James Jackson, a tramp, was again brought up on remand, charged with attempting to break into the lock-up shop of Mr. Brooke, tailor, Waterloo - road, on the 18th of August. He was again remanded. YirIDNBS PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. W. D. Holt. DnuNK AND DISORDERLY. George Hosker, Bridget Murphy, Peter Ashcroft, Adam Butler, Mark Walsh, John Mitchell, Mary Findlone, Henry McKinley were each fined for drunkenness.—For fighting in Warrington-road, on the 26th June, Patrick Coffey, was bound over to keep the peace.—Margaret Redmond was ordered to find the usual sureties for committing a breach of the peace.— On a like charge Mary Ann Connor was bound over. A WOODEN SDlT.—Mary Glover, a married woman, was charged with threatening to assault Elizabeth Stanley. The complainant alleged that on Monday morning the defendant threatened that if she would come out of the house she would make her want a wooden suit in less than five minutes. She had a poker in her hand.—The defendant was bound over to be ef good behaviour for two months. THREATENING A LODGING-HOUSE KEEPER. John Lally, a powerful-looking man, was charged with using threats to William Jones, lodging-house keeper, Lugedale- road, on Saturday night. The defendant said he was drunk at the time, and did not know what he said.—He was or- dered to find sureties for his good behaviour, or go to Saul 14 days. ALLEGED BURGLARY.—John Toonev, a young man, was charged with breaking into the dwelling-house of Thomas Brady, Widnes-road, and stealing several articles of cloth- ing. Mr. Knowles-appeared for the prisoner who had been twice remanded. Superintendent Barker said there was a strong case of suspicion, but the evidence was not so clear as he thought it would be. He therefore asked for the pri- soner to be discharged.—The prisoner was discharged.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MoND&Y.--Before Messrs. Charles Reynolds, A. Thomas, P. Rigby, and Rev. E A. P. Campbell.

PERMISSION To Sm.-L.—William Davis granted permission to sell at the Camden Hotel in Surrey-street. DRIINEENNESS.—AIice Hampson, for being drunk in High-street, on Saturday, was fined 5s and costs. A Sumer.—Robert Jones was charged, that he being a suspected person, was found on the docksof the Bridgewater Navigation Company, on Sunday, with intent to commit a felony. P.C. Breeze deposed to finding the prisoner on board the Florence Louisa, and Mr. Wilson, captain of the Emily Wynn, stated that the prisoner also boarded his ves- sel. In answer to prisoner the captain admitted that the prisoner had worked on his vessel for nearly two months, but was paid off on Saturday.—The cook of the Florence Louisa said the prisoner went on board the vesgel and tried 1 the locks of the forecastle. The prisoner was discharged.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. At Portumna the police are partially boycotted. They are obliged to shoe their own horses, and the bread supplied are getting scarce. Sir Redvers Buller, the newly-appointed special resident magistrate for the counties ef Clare and Kerry, commenced his duties on Monday in the county Kerry, where his head- quarters will be the town of Tralee. Apart from his appout- ment as a political one, it has caused the greatest dissatis- faction amongst not only the resident magistrates of the counties, but the constabulary authorities. General Buller, who is well known amongst the official classes in Ireland, and who is also very popular, will not receive straightfor- ward assistance; for persons, no matter who they are, do not like to be superseded, and this is the light in which his appointment is viewed in the south-west of Ireland. The movement! of the General are to be kept extremely private. T/ro special detectives from the Dublin department were placed with him as protectionists, and they are to accompany him through Kerry. The General, it is stated, objects to , this. There is no doubt that Sir R. Bullet's visit to Ireland ' will in every sense be a most remarkable one.: On Monday morning General Sir R. Buller, accompanied by his private secretary. Celonel Turner, left Dublin for Tralee. He wishes it to be understood that he has not I undertaken a dragooning mission or to carry oat evictions, but to put down moonlighting and ensure the safety of life and property, which he purposes doing by means of flying patrols, communicating with outposts and headquarters. A gonboat is places at the disposal of Sir R. Bailer. By means of this vessel Sir R. Buller can reach any part of the coast. It is stated warrants have been issued against seventeen per- sons. On Sunday night, the house of a farmer named Brosnan, at Curra, two miles from Castleisland, was entered by moonlighters, who, after some parley about his having paid his rent, made him stand up and shot him in the back. Two arrests have been made. The same gang afterwards attacked the house of a man named Rooney, pulling him from the bed, forcing him upon his knees, and firing over his head. Early on Sunday the Droumdeveen tenants of Mr. Jevers. of Glenduff Castle, were visited in turns by an un- known individual, who appeared disguised and armed, and who warned them under a severe threat not to pay their rent. This incident is locally regarded as the more surprising because the greater number of the devers tenantry are poor, and pay their rents to the landlord in work. There was a somewhat turbulent feeling manifest on Monday night on the Shankhill-road, Belfast. Some of the constabulary resumed their duties on the road, where, how- ever, military detachments still remain. The Mayor has issued a proclamation announcing that the police will re- turn to their full duty in the disturbed districts; calling upon all peaceable inhabitants to assist in the preservation of the peace, and the protection of property; and stating that law and order must and will be fully enforced. In accordance with the Mayor's proclamation, the Belfast police on Wednesday morning, for the first time during the past three weeks, were on regular beat duty. In the Shank- hill district considerable crowds gathered, but there was little excitement. Great anxiety was manifested as to how this step would be received when people returned from work. Telegraphing later, a Belfast correspondent reports a renewal of the conflict between the people and the police. Stones were thrown and shots fired at the constabulary, who charged the mob and arrested 15 persons. Archbishop Croke, sending to the Irish Parliamentary Fund £360 received from Dr. Cleary, Roman Catholic Bishop of Kingston. Canada, as a tribute of sympathy and sustainment from his flock and others, Anglicans and Pres- byterians, in the efforts for Ireland's right to self-legis- lation, points to Bishop Cleary's picture of the happy Home Rule of Canada, and asks conversely, "How can we Irishmen be happy in our native land since we do not en- joy the fruits of onr industry? The lands we laboriously till are not our own, and the laws we are expected to obey are not of our own framing. The fields on which we live and labour belong for the most part to those who despise us and bate us. The fruits of our industries are in a great measure consumed by a favoured and frivolous oligarchy, who have done nothing to produce them, and our laws, manufactured by strangers, are enforced often at the bayonet point by foreign mercenaries or Irish-born slaves in the in- terest of a petted and retentions class instead of for the use and benefit of the whole people. How can we be happy? We are strangers and castaways in our own

ANOTHER AGRARIAN MURDER. A young man named Macnamara, son of a farmer resident at Mount Baily, county Clare, was shot dead on Tuesday night. Three lads were arrested on suspicion. A later telegram says that the reason assigned for the crime is that deceased was working for a farmer named Stephen Littleton, who in 1880 took a farm from which the former tenant had been evicted. The Littletons had continued to hold the farm since that time, despite the fact that they had been boycotted and subjected to her forms of inconvenience. On Tuesday night a serious fracas took place in Armagh between a number of soldier e of the Royal Irish Fusiliers and the townspeople. Some soldiers were knocked down and kicked. It is alleged that some of the soldiers expressions, which were resented by the cuisved disloyaliiianB. MESTING or RADICALS. Between 30 and 40 Radical Members of Parliament met on Tuesday, under the presi- detacy of Mr. Illingworth, to discuss the best means of furthering Mr. Gladstone's policy during the coming recess and in the next session of Parliament. A strong feeling was expressed in favour of energetic action, both in the House and the constituencies, in pressing forward Radical measures. THE TITRE WAR IN WALEs.—Further seizure of farmers' stock were made on Thursday, at Llanarmon, in execution of distresi warrants granted for non-payment of tithe-rents. An Anti-Tithe League is being formed by the agriculturists of Denbighshire and the adjoining counties, with the ob- ject of resisting the payment of tithes and compensating farmers who may be levied upon for refusing to discharge the obligation. •
