div.head: HOLIDAY RHYME OF A ROUND
div.p: A HOLIDAY RHYME OF A ROUND

IN WALES. My dear Old Chum,—so you want to know How the holiday went—whether fast or slow. It was just, my boy, A spell of true joy; From beginning to end, we'd a gay old time of it, As I guess you'll say when I've finished my rhyme of it.

There were friend "A" and,me, and.our wives, you see, Bent, as Waugh somewhere says, on a bit of a spree"; And the way we laughed, And the way we chaffed, At rhymes and puns that were broken-backed, You'd have said—" Dear me It's plain as can be That jokers as well as jokes are cracked!' 'Tis a pretty long ride on the Cambrian line To Aberystwith, but 'tis really fine. Talk of change of scene! There's a change each minute; And there isn't, in truth, a dull mile in it. We have many a glimpse of the Severn river— How its beauty makes one praise the Giver! We rush by stream and by wooded glen; We pause by the busy haunts of men; We near at length the mountains high Whose summits appear to cleave the sky; Then gaze on the Dovey, and now the, sea With the sun shining on it right cheerfully; And at last we steam through a fertile vale That cannot have known a winter gale, Till, all alive, by the lively sea Aberystwith is reached—and in time for tea. Did we like the place? 0, didn't we though, Whilst owning some people would call it "so-so." Few donkeys or bands, Or "Aunt Sally stands, Are found on the sands; For the sea being always as 'twere within reach, There's no wide expanse in the way of a beach. It isn't, in short, Like our Southport, Where visitors get telescopic assistance, With an eye to a view of the sea—in the distance. No; the sea's "all there;" And I do declare That it hugs the shore like lake or " llyn There's a tidy tide, and it's always in. And what walks there are! The Castle ruin, Is one of the prettiest spots for " viewing ;" Though, for wider range, it is better still, To get upon Constitutional Hill. 0 it fills one's eyes With glad surprise, For nought can be grander in its way • Than this glorious view of Cardigan Bay. It stretches—aglow with the sun the while— From. St. David's Head to Bardsey Isle; While south, east, north, you have hills up-piled, In a way especially Welsh and wild— With, towering there in the soft blue haze., Proud Snowdon, the monarch of all he surveys. And then beside, If you want a ride, You needn't be ever a moment idle— There's plenty to see on the Ystwith and Rheidol ; While, if you want something that startles and thrills, There's the Devil's Bridge in the heart of the hills. That bridge—oh, it spans a terrible glen, Which well may serve for Old Clootie's den. And there close by— I tell you no lie— Is the Devil's Punch Bowl, And, "upon my sowl," As Paddy would say, In his own choice way, To see it would make you shake in your shoes, Or anyhow give you a fit of the blues; For the water comes crashing, And hissing and splashing, With a leap and a bound, and a fiendish uproar, A hundred times worse that it does at Lodore.

Continue your drive And you quickly arrive At Pont Erwyd where you can, if you like, Turn from the main road and for Plinlimmon strike. We didn't that day Take a turn that way. For myself, having been on the top of Scawfell, And climbed, years ago, Cader Idris as well; Having, too, fully realised Snowdon's great height, I thought, don't you see, How polite it would be To leave Plinlimmon to some other wight. . Would you turn about For another " out ?" Well, down the south shore, Some four miles, or more, There's a place called Monk's Cave, Where the wild waters rave, When the wind is strong and the tide is high. We saw it in calm of sea and sky; But such sign was there of stress and shock, In battered and dislocated rock, That we could but exclaim " It is really no wonder The natives call it the Hole of Thunder!" We went by the road ' To the Monk's abode; . But we thought how fresh and how pleasant 'twould be To find a way back by the cliffs and the sea. Jordan's road, it is said, is a hard road to travel, But 'tis easy to this one of rock and of gravel; For the reefs are here and the reefs are there— They are round about you and everywhere; And you get such shocks With the slips on the rocks, Tou would take it as kind to be put in the stocks. My prudent friend "A," After making essay For a rough half-hour or so, bade me " Good day;" He said he preferred to go miles further round, With some hope of getting home safe and sound. How I struggled through it, and got back—well It was—" here I slipped," and "there I fell ;" It was bad as that burning marl in hell , , Of which we hear John Milton tell. And the "straight tip" is—to put it in brief- -1 You go by the road and avoid the reef. Another day, and we all had a sally (By train) as far as the Llyfnant Valley. 'Tis a place where the fays Might spend their days ; Wood, water, and rock; a romantic glen— Some three miles long, I should tell you, but then 'lt seems so short—for it's all "on the mend"— You are really sorry to know it must end; And as to the end—just think of it all— Rocks, ferns, and flowers, and a waterfall!

Afire on Wednesday night broke out in the Oak Mount Mill at Burnley, and was not extinguished until damage had been done amounting to about £lO,OOO. Two or three hundred people will, in consequence, be thrown out of work.

ALLRMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—An accident occurred to a crowded excursion train from Cheltenham on Monday, at Manßotsfield, near Bristol, on the Midland Railway. The train arrived safely until just outside the station, when some Roods trucks on one of the crossings caught the hin- dermost carriages of the passenger train' smashing in the end of the guard's van and breaking the collar bone of a guard named Quick, and severely injuring another, as well as a little girl. Quick's life is despaired of. Many of the pas- sengers were much shaken.

Miss VIOLET CAMERON ACIAIN.—At the Bow-street Police Court, on lirednesday, Mr. De Bensande, husband of the actress known as Miss Violet Cameron, applied for a sum- mons against Lord Lonsdale for having issued a libel upon him. The libel complained of appeared in the " Topical Times," and was contained in a report of an interview be- tween a correspondent of the paper and Lord Lonsdale. The magistrate refused to grant the summons, on the ground that there was nothing before him to show that Lord Lons- dale authorised the publication of the libel. BRITISH ASSOCIATION. The British Association began its annual session at Birmingham, on Wednesday, when the opening address was delivered by the president, Sir Wm. Dawson. In the course of his address he sympathised with Sir Lyon Playfair's appeal at the Aberdeen meeting in favour of scientific education. Referring to the system of philosophy associated with the names of Darwin, Spencer, and Wallace, he acknowledged its influence on scientific thought. After other general observations, he addressed himself particularly to tha geological history of the North Atlantic, cealing with the question as to whether the At. lantic had achieved its destiny and finished its course. He I said that the stupendous volcanic phenomena manifested I along the borders of the Atlantic in early times had appar- ently died out. These facts were guarantees of perman- ency. Renewed volcanic action in the future was probable, hut to us the Atlantic was practically a permanent ocean The addresa was frequently applauded. itaaammerts—whose professional labours necessitate long In- terval g between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating, comforting, and capable of sustaining exhausted natwe us Cadbury's Cocoa, guaranteed absolutely pure. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. HALF-YEARLY MEETING OF SHARE- HOLDERS.

The second ordinary general meeting of the share- holders in the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held at noon, on Tuesday, in St. Jamee's Hall, Man- chester. There was a very large attendance. Mr. Daniel Adamson (chairman of the company) presided, and was supported by the following directors :—Sir Joseph C. Lee (deputy-chairman), Mr. W. H. Houldsworth, M.P. Mr. Henry Boddington, Mr. James E. Platt (Oldham), Mr. Alderman Husband, Mr. Alderman W. H. Bailey, Mr. William Fletcher, Mr. James, and Mr. Joseph Leigh (Stockport). The following letter, addressed to the caairman, was read by the Secretary (Mr. A. H. Whitworth), and evoked hearty applause:— House of Commons, August 30, 1886. Dear Sir,—l regret not to be at the meeting to-snorrow. You know how strong is my conviction of the necessity of this enternris... It has triumphed over many and great difficulties, and will, I believe, triumph over this last diffi- culty. JACOB BRIGHT. The secretary read the report of the directors for the half-year which ended OR the 30th June last. , After dealing with the accounts, the report went on to say, after explaining the reception the advertise- ment of the prospectus met with:—The directors, acting under the advice of Messrs. Rothschild, an- nounced the withdrawal through the Press on the 24th July: All sums paid on application for shares upon the terms of the prospectus issued by Messrs. IRothschild have been returned to the applicants. In I consequence of the unsuccessful attempt to secure the balance of the capital, the directors have considered it desirable that the future prospects of the company shall he carefully examined before the project is again placed before the public. With this object, on the 28th July they appointed a consultative committee to take into consideration the whole scheme of the Ship Canal Company, including the obtaining of the capi- tal, the strengthening of the position of the company in public estimation, and any other matter affecting the future of thascheme, and to report to the board., The committee, as constituted, was to consist of three members of the board, three outside Manchester men, and two brokers, with power to add to their number; and the chairman, deputy-chairman. and Mr. W. H. Houldswerth, M.P., were appointed to represent the board, and were authorised to elect the other I members of the committee. The directors feel confi- dent that if a well-considered and determined effort be made, backed by Manchester generally, and if the shareholders in the company will give the board as- sistance by pointing out to their friends the remuner- ative character of the investment, by increasing their I holdings in the company, and by bringing in additional shareholders, any necessary outside report will be obtained, and the canal will soon be com- menced." The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the re- port, said he would rather have appeared before them under more auspicious circumstances, but he felt sure the shareholders would sympathise with the board in the grievous disappointment they had experienced. In order that the scheme might be successfully floated it was necessary to interest not only the great traders of Lancashire, but the owners of property along the line of the canal. He bad reason to hope that those whose property had to be purchased would take part of the purchase money in the form of share capital., He was glad to say that the proprietor of the hall in which they were met had not only given the use of his hall free of charge, but had announced to him that he was prepared to take in shares three-fourths of the purchase money of the Pomona Gardens, upon which it was proposed to construct one of the docks. (Cheers.) He hoped that many other owners of land would follow Mr. Reilly's example. He felt confident, as he had taken occasion to say more than once, that , not only the adjoining landowners, but owners of 'land at a distance from the canal, would benefit ver largely from the carrying out of this great I under- taking. There was any quantity of money in the country, and if Lancashire did her duty other parts of the country would follow her exauiple. He had the utmost confidence that if they got 2i to 3 millions in the northern counties they would be able to get through London the remainder of .the sum that was needed to construct the canal. He felt as thor- oughly convincei as ever of the ultimate success ot the undertaking. (Applause.) He begged to move the adoption of the report which had been read. (Loud applause.) Sir JosEPE C. LEE, in seconding the resolution, said that when they saw Messrs. Rothschild, since the withdrawal of the issue, they told them (the directors) that it was essential that Manchester should show her confidence in the canal if money was to be got from London, and the way to show that confidence was by subscribing between two and three millions of money. Now, ManAester had not to the present time supported the ship canal enterprise as she should have done. They had had a great many warm friends, but still in some quarters they had been what he might call "damned with faint praise." They had had a great, many who had criticised the undertaking with- out having studied the enterprise or without having read the evidence—(hear, hear,)—and therefore they thought that the best course they could pursue was to obtain a committee of gentlemen who were well known for their probity and well known for their ability in this community. They were not particular whom they put on; they were willing to put on that com- mittee their antagonists, because they felt that the more the question was studied the more convinced would that committee become, and the greeter sup- port would they obtain from the public. (Applause.) The last time that they went for their money they were a little bit dazzled by the great name of Roths- child—(hear, hear,)—and they trusted too much to their financial gods instead of putting their own shoulders to the wheel—(hear, bear, and applause)— and sloing their utmost in the vicinity of the canal. But adversity had taught them a good lesson, and they promised that the next time they came before the shareholders with their prospectus it would be with some support from the merchants, the property own- ers, and the working people of Manchester. (Loud applause.) Mr. W. H. Houldsworth, M.P., said allusion had been very properly made to what their Liverpool friends called the "financial failure ' of the ship canal. He thought they might have waited a little bit before coming to that conclusion. His own feel- ing was that the so-called "financial failure " might turn out to be a very great blessing. (Hear, hear.) Ho agreed with. Sir J. Lee that a great mistake was made in trusting to the gods of finance, and he felt

NOTES BY THE WAY.

The results of the cricket season leave been highly satis. factory, and our various county teams have been able to hold their own with the Australians, and in several in. stances secured a substantial victory. Lancashire, although nut quite FO successful as in previous years, have played 14 matches, won five, lost five, and drawn four. A. great batting triumph was achieved at Gravesend on Wednesday by the South of England Eleven against the Australians. The home team, who after following on 129 behind on Tuesday afternoon bad made 100 runs for the less of Mr. Pattersen's wicket, went on batting at a quarter to twelve, and were not dismissed until 20 minutes past five, the total amounting to 450. The honours of this perform. ance were due in some degree to nearly every member of the side, bat the chief credit belonged to Frank Hearne, Maurice Read, and W. W. Read. Hearne scored 111, Maurice Read 109, and Mr. Walter Reid 87. With the close of the innings, the match was abandoned as a draw. The Austra- lians were set 322 rcns to get to win, so that they could certainly claim no advantage. A draw was the result on Saturday of the match at Brighton between Sussex and the Australians. In the end the Australians were 148 runs ahead with three wickets to go down. In the three days 27 wickets fell and 852 rum, were scored. There was s.mne fine batting in the match, and some very bad mistakes in the field.

The match between Warwickshire and Cheshire ended on Tuesday at Birmingham in a single innings victory for Warwickshire with 136 runs to spare. In just over half an hour, at Leyton, on Wednesday, Lancashire made the necessary 46 runs wanted to will against Essex for the loss of one more wicket, and thus hest the southern county by eight wickets. The not outs over- night were Barlow and Robinson. The former was soon dismissed, but Robinson and Mr. Royle made the remaining runs, and the game, which had been continued at 11-25, was over by noon. Robinson's not out 51 included nine fours and three twos. .

The first-class county season of Lancashire finished 012 Saturday with their defeat by Gloucestershire. Lan. cashire, it may be mentioned, played seven of the other eight leading counties, but did not meet Middlesex. Mr. A. G. Steel did wonderfully when he played for Lancashire, but unfortunately he did not play- often enough to obtain a legitimate average. Mr. Horohy is at the top of the batting with very good figures. and next to him comes Briggs, the rest of the batting coming out-very moderately indeed. Wat- son and Barlow did some wonderful bowling, and Briggswan also useful at times.

div.head: EARTHQUAKE IN THE UNITED
div.p: EARTHQUAKE IN THE UNITED
STATES. GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. CHARLESTON IN RUINS.

America was visited on Tuesday night by an earthquake, which has wrought terrible disaster and caused great loss of life. All along the coast-line from Alabama to New York the seismic disturbance was felt, and at Pittsburg, Cincinnati, Cleveland, Detroit, and Indianopolis, the shocks were alarm- ingly violent. It is from Charleston, however, that the most distressing news is received. On Wednes- day morning it was found in New York that no communication could be obtained with the southern city; but subsequently a telegram was received in which it was stated that the streets of the town were blocked with fallen houses, that fires had fol- lowed the earthquake, and that 60 persons were believed to have perished. Pame prevails through- out the affected district. In New York and at Brooklyn, where shocks of ten seconds' duration were experienced, people gathered in the open streets and squares; and at Savannah and Augusta negroes were seen in the open kneeling in prayer. A futile attempt at escape was made by the con- victs in the Richmond Penitentiary. At Longley, South Carolina, a mill-dam was destroyed, and, the waters flooding the railroad, a train was over- whelmed, and the engineer and stoker were drowned. At Tybee Island lighthouse the lenses of the lantern were broken; and, fearing a tidal wave, the inhabitants of the island were panic- stricken.

Telegraphing from New York on Wednesday night, the "Daily News'" correspondent says :—A shock of earthquake was felt between nine and ten o'clock last night throughout the whole region of the Unitecl States between the Mississipi River and the Atlantic Ocean. It was especially severe in North and South Carolina, reaching its climax in the city of Charleston, where it caused terrible destruction. The city is wrecked, and the streets encumbered with masses of fallen bricks and tangled telegraph and telephone wires, making it almost impossible to pass from one part of the city to another. Most of the people with their families passed the night in the streets, which even this morning are crowded with men and women, who are afraid to re-enter their houses. .More than 60 persons, chiefly coloured, have been killed and wounded. Fires broke out in different parts of the city immediately after the earthquake, and some are still burning, but there is no danger of their spreading. There is no way of leaving the city at present. It was some hours before any information could be obtained, as all the telegraph operators had fled in terror. The damage in _other parts of the country is trifling. The wave is reported as passing from north to south, and the time of the successive shocks varies from a few minutes, past nine till ten o'cloak. ANOTHER EARTHQUAKE SHOCK.. [CENTRAL NEWS TELEGRAMS.] NEW YORK, THURSDAY.—Another shock of earth- quake was experienced at Charleston at a quarter to 12 last night. It was preceded by an ominous trembling or vibration, then a loud rumbling, and finally quite It severe shock. Many of the houses previously cracked collapsed, and the panic among the people was renewed in its most intense form. _

To add to the general misery there, food in the town is scarce. There is no communication witb the outside world. The rails are twisted and coiled up like pieces of wire, and no trains have reached the city for over 36 hours. A famine is feared. Many are sleeping on board the steamers in the harbour, but the.majority are encamped in the fields. Little has yet been done to clear away the falling (fibril. Many of the streets are absolutely impassable, and it is believed certain that the loss of life will be much greater than the first reports indicated. The superstitious terrors of the negroes have ma(.e them perfectly helpless in this emergency. Great anxiety is felt for the safety of certain Southern to iniships from which no reports have yet been 'received. NBW YORK, THURSDAY, 3 A.m.—Despatches have been received from Summerville showing that the town is safe. Earthquake shocks were experienced there on Tuesday night, and another one at mid- night last night. Little damage was done, but the people were seized with panic. Three-fourths of the building; in Charleston are• more or less shattered.

[REUTER'S TELEGRAM.] NEW YORK, TEtURSDA.Y, 3 A.M.—A despatch re- ceived here from Charleston this morning states that, although the exact number of casualties 15 still unknown, it is believed that from 30 to 40 per- sons have been killed and over 100 injured. The damage to prOperty is estimated at 8,000,000 dollars. There was very little shipping in the port of Charleston when the earthquake occurred, and none of the vessels suffered any damage, the water in the harbour remining unaffected, although all the shocks came from a south-westerly diNction. There have been no signs of a tidal wave. Another shock was felt at Charleston at 11-50 last night, more severe in character than any since the second shock on the evening of the 31st ult. Several more houses fell. -

WASHINGTON, WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON.—Pro- fessor Powell, director of the Government Geologi- cal Survey here, states that the present seismic convulsion has covered an unprecedented area, and has visited many localities which have hitherto en- joyed .complete immunity from earthquakes and volcanic disturbances. He believes it originated in Asia, whence it crossed the Pacific, caused the out- break of the Yellowstone geysers, and then crossed the American continent. Professor Powell adds that the convulsion will probably cause a great tidal wave to cross the Atlantic, and he expects to receive reports to that effect from Europe.

A HATDOCK SERVANT IN TROUBLE.—At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Friday, a respectable-looking young woman named Margaret Ellen Lawrenson, aged 19, Haydock, was charged with stealing one silk scarf, three woollen shawls, one nightelress, one cap, two silk shawls, four pinafores, one pillow-slip, four rh.pkins, one table cloth, four toilet covers, two aprons, one robe, four handkerchiefs, two pairs of kid gloves, one sc trf, one stool cover, one pair cuffs, one strap, and other articles, together of the value of £3 4s, the property of Isaac Brocklehurst, of 55, Denton's Green-lane. —Mrs Brocklehurst said the prisoner had been employed by her as a general servant for the last four months. Prisoner went to bed about ton o'clock on the previous Tuesday night and on the following morning she found the prisoner had gone away. At the time she did not miss anything, but later in the day she went to the prisoner's mother, at Haydock, and whilst in the house she saw the cover of a piano stool which belonged to her. She told prisoner's mother it was hers, and asked if she had anything else of hers. She afterwards found other articles which be- longed to her. The prisoner was not there, and they had heard nothing of her. She went to prisoner's sister's house, and found some more of her property. She found the pri- soner there, and they went together and visited the nonce of one of the prisoner's aunts, and got s Nero! of the articles produced. She thought that the pilfering had been going ore for a month or two.—F.C. Caunce stated that he apprehended the prisoner, who admitted her guilt. —The magistrates stated that they would take into con- sideration her previous good character. She was sent to gaol for a month.—On hearing the sentence, the prisoner cried bitterly.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescet Board of Guars. diens was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present Mr. J. Lowe (chairman), Rev. T. Chambers, Rev. T. Finegan, Messrs. Wm. Birchall, James Jackson, James Buckley, Jobs Matthews, Edward Syder, Charles B. Johnson, Wm. Mid" dlehurst, James Birchall, James Ranson, E. Gerard, Joseph Ellison, J. Kenwright, John Leatherbarrow, Win. Daine.—' The Workhouse Meter reported that there were 451 iU mates this week, agabest 458 last week and 411 in the car' responding period lest year. Vagrants relieved during the week 69, against 55 in the corresponding period of last year. very satisfactory report on the condition of the work' house was read from the Commissioners in Lunacy. letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that they saw no objection to Mr. J. Treaty, relieving' officer, being transferrel from St. Helens to Widnes. nurse having resigned, it was decided to appoint another at a salary of £3O per annum, "without beer."—On the me' tion of the Rev. Thomas Finegan, it was decided to re' appoint Dr. Cooper medical officer of the Widnes lower die" trict for.twelve months, at a salary of £7O pr annum.--• The Clerk read a communication from the Local Govern' ment Board, dated the 19th August, in which was enclosed a copy of a letter from the town clerk of St• Helens to the Local Government Board in regard to the eost of maintaining pauper cases of infectious disease in the St. Helens Borough Hospital. The letter stated that the Corporation had now offered to receive pauper patients for the sum of 4s 6d per day in respect of each case, and that this proposal bad been rejected by the guardians. "The board," the letter Went on to say, "have already expressed the opinion that it is very desirable, in order to the proteC• tion of the district from the spread of infectious diseases that the hospital accommodation provided by the sanitari authority should be made available for pauper cases of such disease. The board trust, therefere, that the guardians will reconsider the matter with a view, if possible, of uric' ing at an agreement with the Town Council as regards the payment for each pauper pa' tient received into the Borough Hospital. ..."• Mr. Jackson remarked that the offer of the Guardians 10 pay 3s a day per patient was a very reasonable offeee.--afr. Daine asked bow ?be matter stood between the Corporation and the Guardians.—The Chairman said that was for the Local Government Board to decide.—The Clerk said the Guardians had not consented to the Local Government Board being arbitrators between the two bodies.—Mr. Daine remarked that 3s a day was a full and sufficient payment W make —The Chairman (who is also a member of the St* Helens Town Council) said he did net think they could do any more until they heard frot° the Corporation, who had probably received a communication from the Local Government Board.l The Clerk said it was evident that the Local Governmerl' Board desired the cruardians to reconsider their position' They first asked the Corporation to reconsider the matters and now they asked the Guardians to do so. The Corpora' ion hail not stated the whole facte of the case. He (tlie clerk) did not think the Leal Government Board would iO s:st upon their paying 4s 61 when they saw that the °the' portion of the union would have to contribute twice over CO! estehlishment charges.—On the motion of Mr. Jackson (S" Helens), seconded Mr. Gerrard (Widnes), the matter left in the hands of the clerk. This was the principal business.

div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

A gentleman of colour—A painter. Burglar's advertisement—Goods carefully removed. No bald-headed men are enlisted now in the American Army; it has been found that it aggravates the Indians. "Hallo, Jack, you're looking down in the mouth! How's the world treating you?" "It isn't treating me at all. I have to pay for myself." What is more pathetic than to see the simple faith with which a bald-headed man will buy an infallible hair restorative from a bald-headed barber? However successful a man may be in resisting the authority of his wife elsewhere, if they attend an auction sale together he will have to do her bidding. We are beginning to doubt that "economy is wealth." At least we have a good deal of economy piled away which we would like to exchange for a little wealth. A French physician is going to sell a number of de- formed skeletons. They will probably. be bought up by some firm who desires some figure to model fashionable corsets on. A telephone clerk says no woman ever answers a call by telephone without smoothing down her hair, working up a smile, and trying to make a good impres- sion on the transmitter. Jones: "Are you going to Germany, Brown?" Brown: "Yes." Jones: "Take your wife with you ?" Brown:! "No. She is not very well, so I shall leave her at home." Jones: "What are you going for?' Brown: "For my health." If language is worth anything at all it is to reveal thought and feeling, and to draw us together by means, of a more intimate knowledge of one another; and, ift. we use it thus, simply, naturally, and honestly, it will become more and more valuable and trustworthy. An American was once asked by an English acquaint- ance what was the tendency of the liquor laws in New England which prohibit the sale of alcohol to any one not a bona fide traveller. He replied with promptitude that they "tended to a considerable deal of bona fide travelling." ELEVATION NOT QUITE ACCEPTABLE.—A Gladstonite buttonholer, talking recently to a prominent Ulster M.P., said, "Do you know, the Nationalists are great admirers of yours; you ought to join their camp, and they'd soon raise you to the very top of the tree." "Yes," replied the latter. "I'm sure they would; but it would be by means of a rope !" Huxley says there was a time when men walked on all fours. We believe you, Huxley, for we have seen them do it when they were little. There was also a time when man walked on the palms of his hanlis, and held up his legs in the air. The time we refer to is after the boy has been to a .circus and has seen the clown do it. Scene—Edinburgh Exhibition. Elderly dame looking I at the figure of Fame over the grand hall "An' wha's yon gran leddy they's gotten up yonder, John ?" John: "Oh, yon's Madame Fame !" Elderly dame, interestedly: "An' what's she famed for ?" John: " Blawin' her ain trumpet, to be shure!" "Maggie, dear, if I should attempt to spell Cupid, why could I not get beyond the first syllable ?" Maggie gave it up, whereupon William said.: "Because when I came to cu, of course I cannot go farther." Maggie said she thought that was the nicest conundrum she had ever heard. "Have you tried Mrs. Brown's kisses ?" is the start- ling query in the window of a Jacksonville candy shop. Mr. Brown was horrified the other morning to find an answer to the query stuck up on the outside of the win- dow. It read: "Yes, and her hugging, too." How RE FOUND OUT.—" And so you've married a jewel, have you, Tom?" "I have, for a fact, Dick. She's a gem without a flaw." "Bless you my boy. I hope you'll always be happy." "Oh, I know I will. Her cooking is like a taste of glory." "Lucky dog! I'm glad to 'hear it; but you're a man in a million. Mighty few go it blind and fare as well as you've done." "I didn't go it blind." "You don't mean to say you knew she could cook before you committed yourself." "That's just what I did, my boy." "How did you ever find it out ?" "I employed a detective, and he managed to get board in the family." AMBULANCE FIELD EXAMlNATlON.—Scene—Hamilton South Haugh; soldier supposed to have been wounded is brought to surgeon's tent by bearers. Bearer, report- ing: Severe scalp-wound, sir, accompanied with insensi- beelity.--Surgeon : Well, what have you done ?—Bearer: Dressed the wound, sir, and gave him a little whuskey- and-water.--Surgeon : Whiskey-and-Water! How did you expect an insensible man to swallow that P—Bearer : He axed for't, sir! A minister on a visiting-tour through his parish had occasion to pass close to a farm the tenant of which had gone over to the Free Church. To show that he har- boured no ill-feeling, the minister decided to enter. He found the farmer and his wife at tea. Farmer: There's a guid day, minister; ye're jist in time to tak' a cup wi' us. Fill oot a cup, Janet." As Janet complied, the minister remarked, "Your tea-pot runs very slowly, Mrs. MacFarlane." Janet: "It dis that, minister. It's gey like yersel' when ye're preachin'—a sort o' slow in the delivery. PROFESSIONAL ETIQL r.—Two friends met the other day in Piccadilly. "Have you been ill?" asked the first. "You don't look well." " Yes ; I am not feeling alto- gether right. The fact is I have consulted three physi- cians, and they don't seem to agree upon the cause of my malady." 'How is that?' "Well, the first said I had consumption, and the second heart-disease." "And what did the third tell you?" "Oh, he gave me to I understand what the third one always does, that the I other two were asses!"

NEWT3N BREWSTER SESSIONS. The annual licensing session for the Newton Petty Ses- sional Division was held at the Town Hall, Newton, on Saturday forenoon. The magistrates on the bench were Mr. R. Houghton and Mr. W. F. Gooch. The proceedints were of a formal character.—Superintendent Weir, of the Leigh portion of the Division, submitted his report showing the number of licensed victuallers, dz.c., and the number of persons convicted for drunkenness, dtc., during the past year, compared with former years. It was as follows :- 1 11 de 7:1 a 23

The total number of townships was 12, licensed vic- tuallers 47, beerhou es 16, outdoor licenses 10, convictions during the year 1885, 1, during the year 1856 5, increase 4; persons summoned for drunkenness 1885 207, 1886 212, increase 5; persons apprehended for drunkenness 1885 61, 1886 67, increase 6, total increase 11. In the VVarrington Police Division, population 73,126, the number of town- ships was 21, licensed victuallers 132. beerhouses 164, off- licenses 35 ; convictions during the year 1885 3, 1886 13, increase 10; persons summoned for drunkenness dur- ing 1885 719, 1886 602, decrease 117 ; apprehended 1885 411, 1886 371, decrease 40, total decrease 157. Superinten- dent Heywood further reported that there were in the Wigan part of the Petty Sessional Division (which com- prised the townships of Golborne and Havdock), 12 inn- keepers, one spirit grocer, and 19 beersellers (14 on and five off the premises), making a total of 32 licensed persons, who were applying for a renewal of their licenses, being the same as last year. During the year no proceedings had been taken against any of the licensed persons for any offence against the tenor of their licenses, which shows that the licensees have conducted their houses in a satisfactory manner. Eleven persons had been proceedel against for drunkenness on Sundays, and 110 on other days, being an increase of two of the former and a decrease of four of the latter, as compared with last year. There are no applica- tions for new licenses. The proceedings taken for all often' ces were as follows : Apprehended 1885 25, 1886 27; summoned 1885 265, 1886 241, total 1855 290, 1886 268. The Chairman (Mr. Houghton) said there had been a few more convictions during the past year than in the pre- ceding year, but there was not a very large increase. This was in the Leigh division, but in the Wigan division there had been no convictions. All the licenses would be re- newed.—Mr. Buckton (magistrates' clerk) said he was de- sired to state by the magistrates that all applications for licenses would lee granted.—The applicants then retired to one of the lower rooms, where they received their re- newals.

div.head: FUNERAL OF THE VICAR OF
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE VICAR OF

• RUNCORN. The interment of the remains of the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., vicar of Runcorn. took place on Monday amid many signs of regret and respect. The town was in mourning. Flags floated half mast high from several public buildings, the shops of the tradesmen were closed with very few exceptions, and in the centre of the town and along the route of the procession the windows of private dwellings were darkened. When the death of the rev, gentle- man became known on Wednesday evening it was felt that the funeral of one that had occupied such a prominent position in the town for 41 years could not be otherwise than of a public character, and Mr. W. 11. Rogerson, who had charge of the arrange- ments, made most elaborate preparations. The de- monstration was most imposing, and a remarkable tribute to the memory of the vicar. The procession numbered upwards of 600 persons, and when the coaches were leaving the vicarage the front portion was filing over Savage's Bridge. The following was the order in which those taking part were mar- shalled by Messrs. W. Mellor, George Moss, and A. Jordan a-- The Improvement Commissioners. Board of Guardians. Burial Board. School Board. Tradesmen. Magistrates and Gentry. Scholars of Parish Church Day Schools. Teachers of Parish Church Day Schools. Scholars of Parish Church Sunday Sphools. Teachers of Parish Church Sunday Schools. Scholars of Newtown Mission Schools. Teachers of Newtown Mission Schools. Clergy and Choir. Firing Party 2nd Cheshire Itifls Voluntters.
HFAIISE. - P 4 =

2r-id Cheshire R7fle Volunteers. First Carriage. Second Carriage. Third Carriage. Private Carriages. As the cortege moved along, to the solemn7music of the "Dead March in Saul," played by the Volun- teer Band of 24 performers, it was viewed by thousands of spectators, who seemed much im- pressed. The Board of Commissioners was repre- sented by Messrs Speakman (chairman), H J Grice, S Taylor, W Fisher, J Meadowcroft, E Timmins, J W Lightburn, E Marshall, W H Linaker, W G Per- cival, C Dutton, W Wright, and T Boote ; Messrs J R Frith, T Riley, and J D Jones represented the Free Library Committee. The Guardians of the Poor present were Messrs Jno Weir (vice chairman), H Lowe, J Stokes, B Aaron, Kirkham, Hewitt, LI Neild, J.P., T Forster, W Farrell, and Jno Davies, with the officials, Henry Linaker, J Ounnah, T Riley, Wlt De Prez P Jones, W Farrington, T Stubbing, T Houghton,Wght, and Dr Carruthers. For the Burial Board, Messrs. Jas Handley, J.P., H Coleburn, W F Salkeld, W Jones and W Ford, attended, and the School Board was repre- sented by Messrs Jas Pritchard, Vice-Chairman, Father Fennelley, R Lea, W Handley, W Howard, and Inglesfield. Amongst the tradesmen were the following; Messrs. They were preceded to the chancel by the choir, who chanted the first portion of the burial service with measured cadence. The service in the church was most impressive, its solemnity being added to by the gloomy surround- ings, the pulpit, communion, and the choir stalls being draped in black. The sacred edifice was crowded, amongst those present being Sir Richard Brooke, Bart.; Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P.; Lady Greenall • Mr C L Evans, representing Major Orred ; Rev E A P Campbell, J.P. • Rev E Marsden, M.A., Vicar of Aston; Rev W Fielding, 8.A., curate of Aston; Rev A P Reynolds, Kingsley; Dr. Steele, Mr William Hayes, Mr Thomas Banks, Mr C Reynoas,J.P. ; Mr A Thomas, J.P.; Mr F Rigby, J.P.; MGL Wie•g,.Mr W Whittaker (people's war- den), Mr 141 A Lake (vicar's warden), Mr M Barker and Mr E Marwood (sidesmen), Mr T T Clint, Liver- pool; Mr G F Ashton, Mr R B Toft, and Mr E A Chorlton. The lessons were read by the Rev H Grantham, and the choir:, under the leadership of Mr Johnson, the organist, sang a psalm and several hymns. The body was borne from the church to . the grave by Messrs John Brock, G- Hitchmough, Jas. Marsh, Thomas Houghton, Joseph Shaw, Richd. Roberts, George Williams (deceased's valet), and E Dunbavand. At the grave side the burial service was conducted by the Dean of Chester at his special request, and the coffin was lowered into quite a bower of flowers, the side of the•grave being covered with flowers, the work of loving hands. After the benediction the choir sang the favourite hymn of the deceased, commencing— Jesus lives! IVO longer now Can thy terrors, Death, appal us. The solemn ceremony was brought to a close by the volunteers firing three volleys over the grave. VOTE OF CONDOLENCE. At the adjourned half-yearly meeting of the Run- corn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company, held on Monday afternoon, the Chairman (Mr. W. Hayes) proposed that the secretary be directed to write to the family of the late Rev. Canon Barclay expressing the sympathy of the Board with them in their bereavement.—Mr. P. Smith seconded the motion, and it was unanimously carried.

CONDOLENCE OF COMMISSIONERS. At the monthly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, on Wednesday, the Chairman (Mr. P. Speakman), before- the commencement of the business, referred to the serious loss the town had sustained through the death of their late vicar. It had been his pleasure to know Canon Barclay for a very great number of years, in fact when he was a boy, and although not a member of his congrega- tion he had always had the greatest respect for the late canon. Although a devotee to his own Church, the canon always gave a helping hand to everyone of whatever denomination. With regard to his public utterances, he was sure they were appre- ciated by everyone who heard them, and with what- ever subject he dealt he gave pleasure to, his audi- ence. He proposed the following resolution of condolence :—" That the Commissioners deeply regret the death of the late Rev. Canon Barclay, who for so many years devoted his time and great abilities to all matters affecting the in- terests of the parish of Runcorn; that they tender to the widow and family of the late Canon their sympathy and condolence in the irreparable loss they have sustained."—Mr. H. J. Grice seconded the motion, and said as a Christian, as a clergyman, aud as a gentleman, the Vicar had been everything that any man could wish him to be, and no one could regret the loss that the whole parish had sustained, and especially the family, more than he (Mr. Once) did himself.—Mr. J. W. Lightburn supported the proposition with pleasure. To say anything about the good qualities of Canon Barclay in Runcorn was like painting the lily. His intellect and heart were combined in such a measure that they would be a very long time before they would see his like again. Canon Barclay used his great talents in the interests of the town and they must all deplore his loss.—Mr. Meadowcroft said he was sure every member of the Board entertained the highest respect for Canon Barclay. Having sat under the late canon for a considerable period, he might say that he was one of the most eloquent and most capable preachers of his day, and with regard, to all local matters he had ever given a most gener- ous and general encouragement to whatever move- ment tended to improve the town. He cordially supported the resolution.— Mr. Dobson said lie had known Canon Barclay for forty- years, and he could not say better than that he had served his day and generation, fell asleep, and was gathered to his fathers. The motion was carried unani- mously.
A man named Hope was at Balton on Thureday sen- tenced to seven days' imprisonment for refusing to give evidence.

I have been down in Norfolk, where I have seen a curious crop growing, and growing well, too. One knows it abroad—the large full leaves, the tall graceful spike, and the delicate bloom; but here in England it has hitherto been confined to botanical gardens or foliage purposes., Of course, it is the tobacco plant. I hear that in Kent also it has been largely cultivated, of course in conformity with the recent Government permissions, and that there, too, the crop is good and forward. This new harvest will be cut in a few days, and I suppose long before Christmas 'Englishmen will be smoking some genuine home grown tobacco. To fastidious smokers the prospect will not be altogether a grati- fying one. The English cigar is not popular. But this will be a cigar produced under wholly different conditions. It may be better, or it may be wcrse. It certainly ought to be cheaper. The English cigar is made of leaves grown broad, and shipped over here, and then made up in London or Bristol. It is said the passage over the sea ruins the flavour. There is no reason why English grown cigars should should not be just as good as German. It is not cer- , tainly a very high standard. Sir W. Lawson's story about the eccentric farm • ; servant who hung himself, and whose master when 1 he heard the news exclaimed. "What will he do next?" finds fresh application in the case of Lord Lennox. Lord Henry has long been a trouble to the eminently respectable family of which he was a member. For sixty-five years he has had to be provided for. Whenever it could possibly be done, at was done at the expense of the nation. But poor Lord Henry's constitutional unluckiness was pre- dominent even here. His unfortunate connection with the Lisbon Tramways Company compelled his withdrawal from the Ministerial office to which he had been comfortably inducted, and since then even a Conservative Government could not be induced to find further provision for him. Driven to extremi- ties, Lord Henry two or three years ago did some- thing for himself. He married a rich widow, and received the congratulations of his friends and rela- tions—more particularly his relations who saw an end of their troubles. But it was only the begin- ning of a fresh departure. His old creditors, who had abandoned all hope of getting back their money with due usury, came down upon him as soon as he was married. But the rich wife decline to disburse. Lord Henry was made a bankrupt, and finally crept out of his difficulties on his hands and knees by payment of an instalment of a, few shillings in the. pound. All this was very dreadful to a ducal family, and well might its respectable members ask in despair "What will he do next?" He did something almost worse than what had gone before. Last Saturday, three days before that fixed for the great festivity of the wedding of his nephew, he took to his bed and died. The family, however, were equal to the occasion. In lower circles of life there is nothing more common than the putting off •of a wedding owing to sudden family bereavement. But the great families of Richmond and Gordon, Brooke and Rosslyn, manage these things better. Every- thing was prepared for the feast, and the feast must take place. So on Tuesday, the poor old uncle lying unburied, the wedding gala was held. "Poor Lord Henry !" as everyone who knew him , says when they refer to his pitiful fate, with this last contemptuous kick. It was a mere accident of ;delayed birth that cut out his career for him. Had 1 he been born a few years earlier he would have been Duke of Richmond an Gordon, with houses to live in and lands to live upon. And a most rdspectable, not to say revered Duke he would have made. As it was he bore the life-long curse of lack of pence. When opportunity of earning a pittance was affor- ded him by the political good fortune of his party, he set himself heart and soul honestly to earn it. had &great liking and much aptitude for Admiralty work, and was quite up to the average of Secreta- ries to the Admiralty. A most courteous, kind- hearted man, his spirit was gradually broken by the harsh treatment of the world. But he had his spirts. One took place just before his wedding, when he went out into Egypt with grey whiskers and beard, and came back clean shaven, save for a foppish moustache, with his hair cut in military fashion, and altogether looking, especially from a back View, quite a youth. It was shortly after this he martied the widow. With his many rings his mincing manners (he always dropped a little curt- sey as he 'touched your fingers with the tips of his own), his rakishly worn hat, and his dandy clothes, forty years too young for him, he irresistibly re- called the immortal Mr. Mantalini. But he meant well, did his best, never willingly injured anybody and people bitterly resent this last insult of clang- ing marriage bells over his coffin. This year has seen a revival of the promotion of companies, a phenomenon intermitted for many years. For the last few months new companies have been projected in platoon with varying suc- cess to promoters and benefit to the public. 'There is, however, one important section of the commu- nity which invariably profits by this form of enterprise. That is the London newspapers which have had a fine bar-vest du ring the last few Months. There have been two striking instances where large sums have been lavished in advertisements and fhe original project has fallen thrnnerh. One of these was the sale of Houghton. Lord Cholmondely, it is said, has paid £2,000 in advertising the sale, the property being finally withdrawn in the absence of bidding. A still larger five() was the advertise- ments of the Manchester Ship Canal Company. This was the largest advertising commission of modern times, and the advertisements had to be paid for though the company was not floated. This was a

LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meettng, of this Board was held in the Board offices on Thursdky evening. There were present Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Rogers, Woolley, Forster, Gibbon, Hall, Thomason, Btazendale ; J. T. Ridgway (law clerk). THE BYE-LAWS.—A letter was read from the Local Gov- ernment Board acknowledging the receipt of a letter from the clerk with reference to the cemplaint made by Mr. J. Townend, of Lymm, in respect to the depositing of refuse, and also inquiring as to the steps the Local Board were taking to have a set of new bye-laws issued.—Mr. Hall spoke at length of the necessity there was for the Board to take stringent steps with regard to the depositing of manure in the Board's district.—ln answer to a question. the Law Clerk said that since the year 1875 he had several times brought the matter of new bye-laws before the Board, but it had always been shelved. The cost of new bvselaves would be between £5O and £6o.—Mr. Brazendale said the question of depositing manure would have to be faced, and he also spoke in favorer of new bye-laws being framed. He had got evidence there to show that Lvmm was in a scan- dalous stare; be could not have believed it was in such a state. He suggested that the matter of new bye-laves be thoroughly dealt with at a subsequent meeting, and this suggestion was agreed to. A Numerous PRACTlCE.—Sergeant Harrington, the superintendent of the fire lot ieade, reported that the mem- bers of the fire brigade attended their monthly drill on Monday, the 30th ult. When testing the hydrants fo-tu- nately only the stand and delivery .pipes were used. Had the lose been attached it must have been seriously injured, as they found a fork and sharp pieces of iron, stones, d:c., in. He mentioned this as it was to the interest of all rate- payers to give them immediate information when they saw any children meddling with the hydrants, thereby running the riek of rendering them unserviceable, and of caning serious damage to the hose. He might perhaps be permitted to say that for the future any parson wishing to register as a cowkeeper, dairyman. or milkseller, must apply to the Urban Sanitary Authority, as their power to issue licensee ceased last month.—The Law Clerk said it would be neces- sary for them to appoint an inspector of milkshops, , under the present law, but that could be done at the next meeting. TOE EXAMINER, SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 4, 1886 !Later to the editor. - - HARD TIMES FOR THE POOR. Sir,—I wish, with your permission, to suggest to such of your readers as care to take an interest ia the welfare of the poor, the wisdom and expediency of arriving at some con- clusion hew best to take steps for meeting mod allevia- ting the distresswe are sure to have during the coming winter.

It cannot be expected that the labouring poor will be pre- pared to meet grim want when her haggard viekiee again appears. Year after year has come and gone, and the mournful pry has ever been "What a depressed state trade is in! " I suppose it is quite true that several times during recen.t years, had it not been that we had Isreadstuffs very cheap, we should have been within meaeureable distance of serious disturbances amongst the people. As a matter of fact, the cheapness to which I refer has had to be supple- mented by the charitably disposed, and the difficulty met with, so far, has been—how best to dispense the charity without at once pauperising the poor, giving to the social " wastrels " or neglecting the really necessitous. During last winter a committee was formed, and, ably guided by the Mayor and Mrs. Harrison, it contrived to re- lieve a great number of really deserving cases, but the great difficulty was felt to be the certainty that nurabers of people were applying for relief who could not have estab- lished a right had their cases received persoeal investigation. How te gain this knowledge, and arrange for the establish- ment of a satisfactory system of distributing the charity of the benevolent, well deserves the attention of those inter- ested during the next two or three months. JOHN HALIFAX.

div.head: FRO DSHAM.
div.p: FRO DSHAM.

HORSHS ASTRAY.—On Monday, at Eddisbury Petty Ses- sions, James Blain and Edward Robinson, carters, Frod- sham, were charged with allowing two horses to stray at Frodsham, on the 21st July. P.C. Marshall proved the csse. Robinson, who did not appear, was fined 5s and costs, and Blain 2s 6d and costs.—John Ardern, cattle dealer, Tiverton. was summoned by P.C. Foden for allowing two horses to stray at Tiverton. Fined 2s 6d and costs For a similar offence, William Bebbington, of Frodshatn, was fined ss.

CHINICH PAIIADS AT KINGSLEY.—On Sunday morning the membHs of the F Company of the Frodsham Rifles, tinder the command of Captain Harrison, started from the Town Hall to the Parish Church of Kingsley. The com- pany was headed by the Overton Brass Band. The service at the church was conducted by the Vicar (Rev. A. P. Rey- nolds), who delivered au appropriate address from Joshua 7—" Only be thou strong, and very courageous." On leaving the church the company were put through the usual evolutions. FRODSHAM AND PRODSIIAM LORDSHIP PAROCHIAL Cosit- ItyrraEs —The usual fortnightly meeting of the above Committees was held in the Town Hall. Frodsbam, on Fri- day evening, when Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., presided. The ten- der of Mr. Littler, of Frodsham, for covering the trial wells at Newton, for the sum of £3l 15s Bd, was provisionally ac- cepted. The tender of Messrs. Kirkhain and Co.. of Run- corn, for the Overton drainage extension, amounting to SS 10s., was accepted for this work. There was no other basi• ness of public interest.

FROMHAM AND HELSBY DRAINAGE BOARD.—ANNUAL ELECTION —A general meeting of ratepayers within the dis- trict of the Frodsham and Helsbv Drainage Board was held In the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Wednesday evening, for the purpose of electing new members of the Board. Mr. Henry Bessvick, of Barrow Hall, presided, and there were also present, Messrs. Thomas Davis, Ralph Bate, John Foster, James Percival. and C. E. Linaker, clerk to the Board. The following members were re-elected, viz. : Messrs. E. A. Wright, J.P., William Hayes, James Rey- nolds, James Andrews, Ralph Bate, William Booth, Law- rence Booth, Henry Beswick, Thomas Davies, John Dutton, Joseph Ellams, John Priestner. James Percival, and Thomas Wright. Mr. William Garner was also elected in the place of Mr. John Challoner, deceased. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting. UNLAWFUL POSSBSSION Of GAMIL—At Eddisbnry Petty Sessions, on Monday, Charles Cross, a huckster, of Five Crosses. Frodsham, was charged with being in the unlawful possession of game at Frodsham.—P.C. Darrock proved meeting the defendant on the 14th August. with a horse and cart at Frodsham. Being suspicious, he inqeired what the cart contained, and defendant replied that he had nothing in it but berries and peas. Witness searched the cart, and in a hamper found a number of rabbits. On being ques- tioned about them defendant said he had bought them at Five Crosses, but afterwards said be bad found them in his back yard that morning. On the hamper being taken to Frodsham Police Station, it was found to contain 41 rabbits. —Defendant stated that he bought tue rabbits from a man be did not know. He was not aware he was breaking the the law.—P.C. Darrock informed the Bench that the defen- dant had formerly been a police officer, and therefore knew the law perfectly.—Defendant was fined 45s and costs.
MARRIAGE OF MISS THOMAS AND THE REV. E.
CHARLEY.

The marriage of Miss Margaret Eva Thomas, eldest daughter of Mr. Alfred Thomas, J.P., of Hemp Gill, Nether- ton to the Rev. Edward Charley, M.A., senior curate of FrOdsham. and only surviving son of the late Mr. Edward Charley, Conway House, ca.unty Antrim, took place at Frodsham Parisb Church on Thursday afternoon. The ceremony attracted a large congregation. In Overton, the leafy lanes were bright with flags, while the Union Jack floated from the tower of the Parish Church, now undergo- ing extensive repair. At the entrance to Hemp Gill, the residence of the bride's father, was a handsome triumphal arch. The main supports were decked with heather and foliage, and from the centre of the arch depended the em- blematical pair of white gloves. On one side of the arch was the motto, "May you live long and prosper," and on the other, "Health and happiness." The arch, which had been most tastefully constructed, seas the joint work of the eardeners of Mr. Thomas, Mr. C. Reynolds, J P., and Mr. John Simpson. The bride has endeared herself to the hearts of many of the parishioners by several years' attention to parochial work. Amongst other duties discharged by her she has filled the responsible position of teacher in the National Sunday schools, and the affection of her scholars was displayed by their scattering flowers in the path as the newly-married pair left the church. ' The hour fixed for the ceremony was two o'clock, and long before that time many seats in the church were occa- ' pied. Several hundred spectators remained outside, and lined the pathway from the gates to the porch in order to witness the arrival of the bridal party. The path was covered with crimson cloth, which was continued right through the church to the chancel. The choir stalls were adorned with beautiful flowers. The altar rails were also covered with flowers of choice bloom, and on the commu- nion table were two exquisite crosses of white roses. Seats had been reserved in'the nave for the wedding party. trimly of whom took up their positions at least half an hour before the commencement of the service. Punctually at two o'clock the bride, accompanied by her father and followed 'by her five bridesmaids, entered the church, while the choir, in surplices. sang the hymn, "The voice that breathed o'er Eden." At the chancel arch, Miss Thomas was joined by the bridegroom, while the bridesmaids ic their taster al dresses, formed a charming group as they awaited the arrival of the clergy. The bride's dress had a bodice and I a train of rich white Irish poplin, the white satin skirt hay- ing long draperies, the whole being trimmed with lace. I She wore a tulle veil and wreetb of orange blossom; a gold necklet, the gift of the brideeroom, and other handsome ornaments. The bride also had a beautiful bouquet, and carried an exquisitely embroidered fan. Tbe bridesmaids were Misses Muriel Thomas, sister of the bride, Christian Carter, Kathleen Reynolds, Mabel Tinsley, and Gertrude Crosfield. Their dresses were of cream Surat silk, with princess bodices; the pleated skirts and puffed draperies being trimmed with pale blue satin and Mauresque lace. Their sailor hats were trimmed with cream spotted telle and blue velvet bows to match. Each bridesmaid wore a gold and silver brooch, the gift of the bridegroom, and carried a bouquet of cream roses and pink bouvardias. Nothing could have been prettier than the scene presented to the congregation. A stream of bright sunlight flooded the chancel, and the chaste and charming combination of colour was very effective. The officiating clergy were the Rev. W. L. Paige Cox, 8.A., vicar of St. Peter's Reck Ferry; Rev. Canon Whitley, MA..; and the Rev. R. M. P. Butler, B.A. The Rev. Augustus E. Crowder acted as groomsman. At the close of the marriage service, the bride and bridegroom proceeded to the altar, where the Rev. Canon Whitley offered the usual prayers. The choir then sang " How welcome was the call," after which Canon Whitley pronounced the Bene- diction. The newly-married pair then entered the vestry, where the register was formally signed and attested. On re entering the church, the organist, Mr. Thomas Riley, played Mendelssobn's "Wedding March." As Mr. and Mrs. Charley left the church, ten girls, members of the bride's Sunday school class, scattered flowers in the path. Two children of Mrs. C. E. Linaker, dressed in white, with vel- vet Tarn-o'-Shanter hats, also scattered nosegays beneath the feet of the bride. Quitting the church, the happy pair were showered with rice. The boys of the grammar school, under the charge of Mr. Pollard and Mr. Hutton, lined the pathway, and after spreading flowers in the way, they cheered to the echo. The bridal party were driven to and from the church in several private carriages, place,l at their disposal by gentlemen in the neighbourhood, and three palm supplied by Mr. Roberts, of Frodsbam.

The bride cake, which was a triumph of confectionery skill, was supplied by Miss Bibby, confectioner, Frodshana. It was upwards of four feet in height, and was handsomely ornamented with flowers and emblems. The cake was made in the form of a vase, the stand being covered with silver.

In the afternoon a garden party was elven at Hemp Gill, when Mr. and Mrs. Charley received the congratulations of numerous friends. The Frodsham Brass Band, under the conductorship of Mr. T. Jones, discoursed selections of mu- sic on the lawn.

Mr. and Mrs. Charley left Sutton Weaver Station for Lon- don at five o'clock in the evening. After a short stay in the metropolis they will proceed to Ireland where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's travelling dress and jacket were of navy blue foule cashmere, trimmed with vel- vet to match; straw bat of the same colour, with trimmings of navy blue and sky blue velvet. The entire trousseau was supplied by Messrs. Brown Holmes, and Company, of Chester. The presents rcceived by the bride were very numerous.

The CLERK submitted an estimate of the expenditure for the ensuing half-year, which he estimated would ne covered, taking into account the balance from last half-year, when the rate was Id in the X, by a rate of fd id the X. There would also be calls in respect of special drainage upon the Warrington portion of the Authority's district of £1413. and Penketh £9 I.os.—The estimate was adopted.

div.head: SURVEYOR'S REPORT:
div.p: SURVEYOR'S REPORT:

Mr. OWEN T.( ported that duriag the month inspections had been made of Mr. Bissell's houses in Price-street, Love- ly-lane, Warrington; Mr. J. Davies, additions to house, Hollinfare ; Lord Winmarleigh, two cottages and two farm- houses,Rixton ; Mrs. Ashbrooke's house, Orford, and the Weston Trustees' farmhouse, Rixton. Lovely-lane drain- age district: He had obtained two estimates for a short length ef drain in one of the proposed streets, the only one as yet settled upon by the lessors. He had prepared a plan of the whole of this district with a view to settle the amount to be paid to the Corporation for the right of drainage through their sewers in accordance with the terms of the agreement en- tered into with the Authority. For the year 1885 the rate- able assessment of the land upon which one penny in the £ had to be paid was £22 5s 70, and of buildings, etc., up- On which 4d in the £ had to be paid was £7o4.making a total rateable value for the district of £726 5s 711, and a total amount of payment to be made of £ll 17s 7-1-cl. The con- nection with the Corporation sewers was made in January, 1882, and payments should have beete made to the Corporation for the years 1882, 1883, 1884, and 1885, but owing to the agreement having been by mistake de- tained by the Local Government Board, these payments had not been made and had now to be accounted for. He had made calculations for the four years and found that up to the let of January last there was due to the Corpora- tion the following sums :—For 1882, £5 Cs 1L44 ; 1883, £7 is 3P ; 1884. £8 3s 71 ; 1885, £ll 16s 7-1 d ; total, £32 83 6d; say £32, and on the Ist of January next (1887) there would be an amount of £l2 due for the'curret4 year, 1886.—Cottages at Burtonwood: At their previous meet- ing the authority requested him to report upon the cat-ages in Alder-lane, Burtonwood, occupied by Messrs. Derbyshire, Appleton, and Meran, and owned by the Hon. L. W. H. Powys. The three cottages were in ORO block and under one .roof. On the 12th ult he (the surveyor) isited the cottages with the inspector, and was prepared in every re- spect, to confirm the report he made at their last meeting. In his opinion the cottages were unfit for habitation, the thatched roof was in holes and lets water in, the walls are bulging, the floors aud roof are both propped, and generally tee cottages appear to be so unsafe that he .asked their clerk to write at once to the agent to the estate as his eaey attention to the matter was of importance. The fol- lowing plans had been submitted, and being in accordance with the byelaws, might be approved, viz :—Dr. J. H. Gor- nail, bowie at Grappenball; Mr. J. Millington, two houses and stable, Penketh ; Mr. J. Dobson, five cottages, Lloyd- street. aff Lovely-lane, Warrington •, Mr. Charles Matthews, four houses at Penketh. School Chapel, Burtonwood: He had given permission for the opening of this building as a chapel, but not as a school until such time as plans were submitted and approved, and the necessary outbuildings erected, and also a water supply approved of.—The CLERK said that with regard to the three cottages at Burtonwood, be had written to the agent of the property, who replied that he would inspect the cottages and see whether they could be repaired or should be pulled down.

div.head: AN INQUIRY.
div.p: AN INQUIRY.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board re- ferring to the resignation of Mr. Bawling, inspector, and asking for the reasons of the Authority for reducing the salary to be given to the inspector from £llO to £BO a year. —The CLERK said be proposed to reply to that, that the inspector would be supplied with a uniform in addition to his salary. and further, that when Mr. Bawling WAS ap• pointed they had no surveyor, while they now had an ex- perienced surveyor, which took a great responsibility from the inspector.-1 he CHAIRMAN: There is another reaq'm ; that this Authority think the reduced salary sufficient. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. J. HOUGHTON: There are plenty of reasons.

Belfast was reported quiet on Friday morning, and the police were patrolling the disturbed dititricts without moles- tation. There was no di-turbance. THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.—The sections of the British Association at Birmingham continued their sittings on Fri- day morning. In the Anthropological section the first paper was read by Sir Charles Wilson. who gave a detailed ac- count of various tribes in the Soudan, from notes made du- ring the campaign there. ArrearPrup WIFE Mtranua.—A man who gave his name as John liarrety, and said he was a hawker, was arrested en Friday at Buckingham for having attempted, it is alleged, to murder his wife lay cutting her throat. He was with his wife and a 11,ghland piper at Bicester on Thursday, and, missing the woman, traced her to Buckingham, where he discovered that she was staying with the piper. The woman's throat was badly cut, but it was sewn up. THE WOMEN OF IRELAND AND MR. GLADSTONE.—The declaration in favour of Home Rule by the women of Ire- land, promoted by the Lady Mayoress of Dublin, the pre- sentation of which to Mr. Gladstone has been delayed by the geeeral election an other causes, is to be presented to him at Hawarden, about the 21st, by the Lady Mayoress and some other ladies. It is stated to be of very large dimensions, and to bear nearly half a million signatures. TERRIBLE POACHING AFFRAY.—EarIy on Friday mom- ing an inspector and eight constables from Northwich en- countered supposed poachers at Shipbrook Bridge. The latter immediately showed fight, using, it is alleged, stones, bludgeons, and knives. A vigorous struggle followed, and several of those taking part in it were much injured, especially one of the supposed poachers. Ultimately the police secured five of their assailants, and also seized a large number of hares, rabbits, and implements for taking game.

ALARMING RAILWAY COLLISION AT BOLTO4.—At a quar- ter past one o'clock on Friday afternoon an alarming colli- sion occurred at the Bury Junction, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, at Bolton. The 10-15 express train from La, th to Blackpool was just entering the station when a goods train was passing. The passenger train was crowded with people, and dashed into the goods train, cutting it in two, and damaging many carriages and waggons. No one was hurt, but the lines were blocke4 with the debris and the traffic is impeded.
THE EARTHQUAKES IN THE UNITED STATES

The " Times " Philadelphia correspondent telegeaphs : The official list of deaths .at Charleston includes thirty- three porn& the wounded numbering one hundred. The loss of property is now placed below fire millions. The latest shock felt was at fire o'clock on Thursday morning. The earthquake motion was a twist or turn instead of being simply undulating. Subscriptions for the relief of the suf- ferers at Charleston have been opened throughout the country. Considerable sums have been forwarded, and money is coming in freely. Latest advices from Charleston, telegraphs the Central News New York correspondent, state that the panic is somewhat subsiding. People continue camped in the open squares and parks. There have been no further shocks up to Thursday midnight. Owe half the hons, sin the city will require to be built from their foundations. Some enormous fissures in the earth near Charleston are reported to be continually posting forth hot mud and water. THE BULGARIAN CRISIS. THE PRINCE AT PEIILIPPOPOLIS.

PIIILIPPOPOLTS, THIIRSDLY, 7-30 P.M.—Prince Alexander left at five a'clock this afternoon by train for Sofia, travel- ling via Sarambey. His Highness was accompanied to the railway station by a large crowd of people, by whom he was warmly cheered. It is believed that the Prince intends to grant an amnesty to the conspirators should they ask pardon. _

VIENNA, FRIDAY.—AII this morning's newspapers attach great importance to the telegrams exchanged between the Czar and Prince Alexander. The " Fremdenblatt " gathers from the Prince's despatch that he will abdicate after hav- ing re-established order, his future having become well nigh hopeless.

div.head: SUBMISSION OF REBEL TROOPS.
div.p: SUBMISSION OF REBEL TROOPS.

SOFIA. FRIDAY.—The rebel Bulgorian troops have uncon- ditionally surrendered and have appealed to the Prince's clemency. The statements published in some foreign jour- nals that sanguinary encounters had occurred ' bqtween the Government and rebel troops are wholly unfounded. Tran- quility reins throughout Bulgaria, and public order is at pre- sent nowhere disturbed. PRINCE ALEXANDER AND THE SULTAN.

CONSTANTINOPLE, FRIDAY. Prince Alexander, when passing through Bucharest on bis return to Bulgaria, re- quested the Ottoman Minister to telegraph to the Sultan assurances of his homage and devotion to his Majesty.

div.head: DROWNING FATALITY NEAR WAR-
div.p: DROWNING FATALITY NEAR WAR-

RINGTON. The dead body of a man named William Jackson, who lived in Atherton-street, was on Tuesday even- ing recovered from the canal at Sankey, a short distance from Buttermilk bridge. The .clothes of ' the deceased were found lying on the canal bank, and the matter was then reported to the police,who obtained assistance and dragged the canal. The head of the deceased was stuck in the mud, and the heels were projecting outwards. The body was taken to the Black Horse Inn, Sankey Bridges, where it was identified. It is surmised that de- ceased undressed with the intention of bathing, the day being a hot one, and, plunging from the towing path got fast in the mud, from which he was not able to extricate himself. Mr. W. T. Husband, de- puty coroner, held an inquiry into the occurrence yesterday afternoon, at the Blackhorse public- house, Sankey Bridges. Evidence was called to the effect that the clothes of the deceased were found on the bank of the canal by a man named ' Broadhurst, at about 4-30 on Tuesday afternoon. He took them to the police station at Sankey Bridges, and gave them into the possession of P.C. ' Dugdale, who procured assistance and went to the place where the clothes had been found. The body was recovered by means of a rake by a person named Nathaniel Cooper. of Sankey Bridges, who gave it as his opinion that whilst bathing the de- ceased had been seized with crapip, and could not get out of the water. The jury returned a verdict that the deceased met his death by drowning, prob- ably when bathing.

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB FOR SUTTON.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB FOR SUTTON.

A bench Liberal Club, with the view of strengthening and uniting local Liberals was formally opened at Sutton, near St. Helens Junction, on Monday evening, by Mr. A. J.P., the Liberal candidate at the recent election for the borough of St. Heleas. The premises are situated in Junction-lane, and as an evidence of the need of some such institation it may be stated that over 100 members have al- ready been enrolled.

At the opening ceremony there was a large attendance of of members and friends. Mr. Charles Walsh (chairman of the branch) presided, and said he was proud to think that what was once considered unnecessary, and, in fact, a Utopian scheme, v:z —the establishment of a branch club— had become a fact in East Sutton. He trusted it would not degenerate into a gambling saloon, for if he thought it woeld he should withdraw from it at once any influence he might possess. But be could not anticipate anything of so in- jurious a character. (Applause.)—Mr. A. Sinclair, J.P., was received with cheers. He said be bad heard -with pleasure what the chairman had said. They did not wish to preclude reasonable amusements, but the main object was to keep members well posted in political matters, to Increase their political knowledge, and to encourage them to spread it among their neighbours. (Applause.)-- The Chairman then handed the key of the door of the club to Mr. Sinclair, with which that genileman unlocked and opened the door, and formally declared the club open for the use of the members.

An adjournment was then made to the National Schools, where a public meeting was held, and about 200 persons were present. Mr. A. Sinclair, 1.13., prepided, and was sup- ported by Councillors A. Hanson and J. Forster ; Messrs. Dromgoole, J. B. Leach, H. Martin, W. Smith. F. A. R. Neill, C. Walsh, and others.—The Chairman conartulated them upon the good start they had made, and said it would encourage and inspire the Liberals of the borough gener- ally with fresh vigour. (Applause.) He was glad to hear that Mr. Walsh hail determined to set his face against gambling in the club, because if it were so used, instead of improving the minds of the members in political know- ' ledge, it would simply degrade everyone who meddled with t. He hoped the oemmittee would be determined to keep down everything of that kind. Reasonable amusements they would be glad to see ; it was not amusements but gambling they objected to. He tion!d the members would go there to read the papers and increase their stock of political knowledge. He (the chairman) had the strongest conviction that if people would only read enough there would be nothing left but Liberals in the world. (Loud applause.) Mr. Sinclair then proceeded to speak upon the general subject of registration amendment, in which the ex- Premier was interested, and said he hoped Mr. Gladstone, who was still their greet leader, would remain their leader for many years to come. (Applause.)— Mr. H. Martin proposed " that we, the Liberals of East Sut- ton, desire to express our unabated confidence in the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, trusting he will be long spared to lead the Liberal party in Parliament, and that his efforts to do justice to Ireland may yet be crowned with success." He congratulated the working Liberals of East Sutton on the establishment of the club, and expressed the hope that it would be used as an educational influence in Liberal principles, which principles, they believed, were true and just in the interests of working-men. (Applause.)—Mr. William Smith seconded the resolution. He said be felt confident that if the Liberals of that borough once got united there would never be another Tory member of Par- liament fer St. Helens. (Applause.)—Councillor ILinsan supported the resolution, which was carried unani- mously, the audience giving loud cheers for Mr. Gladstone, and singing, "For he's a jolly good fellcw."— Councillor .1. Ferster then proposed—" That we, the Liberals of East Sutton, are of opinion that the formation of the Liberal Club in Sutton will have a beneficial effect, tending to inculcate, develone, and consolidate true Liberal principles." He said the Lil;eral of St. Helens were not a all disheartened. They knew that right would prevail in the long run, and if thy kept plodding on and doing their best with the registration, the time would soon come when they woeld be able to return a good, sound,and true Liberal for St. Helens. (Applause.)—Mr. Dromgoole seconded the reqolution, which was supported by Mr. J. B. Leach, both of whom urged those present to use their utmost endeavour in the Libc•ral ciese.—The resolution was carried, and a vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings. which were throughout of an enthusiastic nature.
