A VIOLENT PRESCOT MAN AT NEWTON BREDGN.."" Before Messrs. R. Houghton and W. F. Gooch, at the NO' ton Town Hall on Saturday, Henry Stanton, a young Oen residing at Present, was charged with travelling from Liver— pool to Newton Bridge without ticket; also with assaulting Henry Forster and John Jones, railway employes.—Henri Forster, railway porter, said plisoner arrived at Newton, Bridge station by the 11-10 p.m. train from Liverpool oa the previous Saturday. He was under the irfluence of drinke. and had to be pulled out of the cirriage. He refused tO give up any ticket, and struck witness.—John Jones, ticket collector, gave corroborative evidence, and said prisoner would not leave the train. He persisted in saying he Wee going to Manchester. He used abusive lioguage when be got on the platform, and refused to give any account of himself. Prisoner etruck him across the face.—P.C. Spencer deposed that he heard a disturbance at the station, and 011 going there he saw the prisoner strike Forster a violent blovi on the face. Witness locked him up, and found in his p 05.. session a ticket from Liverpool to Prescot --The prisOUst said he had booked from Liverpocl to Prescot, but got in the wrong train. When he arrived at Newton he thought he was at Huyton, near Prescot, and he told the officials he had to go on a licle further. They then pulled him out of the train. He strongly denied having assaulted the official 4 and said as he had been in prison for a week he thought he had had enough punishment—The Bench dismissed the case of travelling without ticket, but imposed a fine of lOs and costs for ;be assaults.

No swine shall be moved Into the Borough of Warring- ton from the oistrict of any other Local Authority unless a Movement Licence be first obtained, which shall only be granted on a declaration being made by the Owner or his Agent to the following effect (1) That such swine has not been elsewhere than on the farm or lauds ft om which the movement is to be made during 28 days immediately preced- ' the date of tbe application for the license. I ought to mention another thing We did one day while on the wing. We doubled back on the Cambrian, As far as Machynlleth, and there our plan Included a run on the Corns lines— Toy engine and carriages up to the mines. Ah, the way thereto It was wholly new— What Lancashire people would call "a rum do." Road, rail, and river are jammed together, As if they would mix in rainy weather. You can step on the road, or jump in the stream, And so very strange does the whole thing seem, It is just like travelling in a dream. So narrow the way, And so little the play, The carriages push green boughs aside In order that Jack and his Jill may ride! As for Corns itself, It is but a big delf : But go a couple of miles or so For a sight as fine as the land can show. Cader Idris, summit and base, is seen, With other mountains, and, snug between, Smooth and bright as a new-made pin, You see one of the beauties of Wales—Tal-y-llyn. We went to Tow-yn for half a day, And heie we loafed the hours away. There are sundry rills And plenty of hills;. I cannot say much of the place but that— • For the coast is like Warrington—all on the flat. Then we sped to Barmouth for two or three days, Where all things seemed in a golden haze; For the harvest sun His work had begun, And he meant to keep at it until it was done. The "Panorama "—you know the scene— Was a lovely vision of shade and sheen, Such as earth might seem to Eve's fair eyes When twilight stole over Paradise. Dolgelley, and not less the Torrent Walk, Will serve for many a future talk; For the day was hot and the shade was cool; And we sat by many a glassy pool; And we heard the river sing its song, iAs it merrily, merrily danced along; Now gambolling by a bank of fern, ' And now, after many a frisky turn Rushing o'er rocks in a white cascaCle, • With a shout of glee at the stir it made, 0, the varied and delicate shades of green— Were ever so many at one glance seen! See the fern By the "burn," And the moss by the tree.-- Could anything sweeter or brighter be! Away and away, On the very next day, By Harlech Castle to liadoc Port, Whore, on iron horse, we pull up short. Short, too, is the stay; Still on and away, But this time we drive, Until we arrive It Pont ..hiberglasyn; its grandeur admire, And the mountains too, which seem nigher and higher. Beeld-gelert we reach, Which a lesson doth teach • Of faithfulness e'en unto death; 'tis a story Which covers this part of the land with glory. Then a trudge of two miles—a trudge did I say? 'Twits a charming saunter the whole of the way Till Dinas was gained—clear lake and clear skies; A sight which must ever be good for the eyes. Ah ! 'tis goo I I vow For mine just now; For I restfully close them, when by them swim Sky. lake, and river, and mountains dim; And 'tis joy to know That, wherever I go,' These pictures will ever be part of me— What the soul thus sees it will always see. • But stop, my friend, We are near the end; It is "Home. sweet home," so I cannot do better Than finish the journey and close my letter. —Eprrom Warrington, Aug. 30, 1886.

Mr. J. HOWARD did not object to give the Government time to consider their measures, but he thought something ought to be done to alleviate sufferings in the coming winter. Mr. A. L. Bum-yr; objected to a policy of immense de- liberation. The case of Ireland was urgent, and, as he be- lieved, something ought to be done to suspend evictions in the 'coming winter, he would vote for Mr. Dillon's amendment. Mr. A. O'CoNNon also supported the amendment. Sir M. HICKS-BEACH claimed for the Governmenl time for deliberation, and contended it was impossible to go fur- ther than they had done as to their legislation. Mr. PARNELL explained the cause that prevented his being in his place to move his amendment. He said it was so urgent that some remedial measures should be at once proceeded with as regarded the land question, and, as the Government only proposed inquiry, he (Mr. Parnell) would bring in a measure himself at once to deal with that sub- ject. It would not go the length of suspending evictions, but it would propose to suspend ejectments on payment of three parts of the rent. If time was given him to do that, be would ask his hosourable friend to withdraw his amend- ment. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUHR said the Govern- ment had announced their views with regard teethe measures they proposed for Ireland, and they would not depart from or alter those views. The member for Cork had responsi- bilities on him that were as great as those of the Govern- ment or any member of that House. He had made his observations in a spirit of moderation, and, if he desired, before the session clesed, to have a special sitting for the consideration of the measure he proposed to introduce, the Government would meet him to that extent. (Loud Irish cheers.) Under such circumstances, be hoped that advan- tage would not be taken of the facilities for objecting to the taming of Supply. Mr. Join; MORLHY thought the Government had adopted a wise course in matting this offer. Some discussion afterwards took place on amendments by Mr. Laboucbere and Major Saunderson. [LHer sirrnge.]
